# Engineering product families with Templates

These examples map the useful Preview 3 envelope. Every example uses an existing compiler or domain path; none adds geometry or a general programming construct.

## Fastener-aware mounting interface

[`generic-mounting-plate.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/generic-mounting-plate.firmament) is a complete product Template parameterized by width, height, thickness, and shaft-hole diameter. It enforces positive dimensions before materialization and produces a deterministic mounting plate through the ordinary semantic Hole path. [`record-array-hole-pattern.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Patterns/record-array-hole-pattern.firmament) extends the idea to a finite `MountSpec` set. Counterbore and countersink families use the same existing `Hole<...>` semantics when that variant is fixed by the family.

## Process-aware machined part

[`cnc-dfm-policy.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/cnc-dfm-policy.firmament) is the complete modern port: typed policy Record, immutable shop defaults, `with` specialization, named positive-limit `Require`, a `CncManufacturingPolicy` Concept Struct, and real minimum-tool-radius enforcement against a semantic Hole. [`boss-pocket-block.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Features/Boss/boss-pocket-block.firmament) demonstrates the existing Boss/Pocket vocabulary; Pocket's explicit `MinimumFloorThickness` remains the local final authority.

The matching [`fdm-dfm-policy.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/fdm-dfm-policy.firmament) and [`sheet-metal-dfm-policy.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/sheet-metal-dfm-policy.firmament) ports preserve the historical nozzle/wall/overhang/layer and thickness/bend/K-factor data as typed family contracts. Persisted lowercase process templates still parse through the compatibility adapter, but new source should use these canonical data-first forms.

## Derived enclosure family

The embedded [`SheetMetalProductFamilies.firmament`](../../../Aetheris.SheetMetal/Firmament/SheetMetalProductFamilies.firmament) is the flagship product-family implementation. `ElectronicsEnclosure<Spec: EnclosureSpec>` changes width, depth, height, thickness, bend radius, K-factor, lip height, and relief policy while retaining one body definition. Desktop and rugged configurations can be derived from one immutable Record with `with` before specialization.

## Table-driven plate family

[`table-driven-mounting-plate.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/table-driven-mounting-plate.firmament) selects a `PlateStandard` from a keyed finite Table, nests it in `PlateSpec`, derives a thicker configuration with `with`, and specializes one profile/Compose family. Its generic parameter is a Record; positive dimensions are the constraint; the concrete plate bounds and thickness change.

[`profile-delta-recess-extrusion.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Profiles/profile-delta-recess-extrusion.firmament) applies the same Table → `with` → typed Template progression to a semantic profile program on an ordinary extruded Model. [`profile-delta-tab-family.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/SheetMetal/profile-delta-tab-family.firmament) consumes the standard-library `Tab` family in Sheet Metal. Together they show that `ProfileDelta` is reusable profile metaprogramming, not a Sheet-Metal-only parser special case.

## Pattern-specialized features

[`four-hole-pattern.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Patterns/four-hole-pattern.firmament) combines `Static` Record data, `Template<spec: MountSpec>`, and `Pattern ... Over`. The same feature Template expands any bounded mounting list into deterministic semantic holes without recursion or a loop language.

## Semantic type specialization

The compiler's canonical Template tests exercise `Template<type TBody satisfies PrismaticBody, Width: Length, ...>`. The type-like parameter is visibly different from values and must satisfy a language Concept. A finite enum `Match` selects an already-supported chamfer distance; the selected branch is erased before Feature AIR.

## Forge automation

`Standard.SheetMetal.ElectronicsEnclosure` exposes the enclosure family through Forge Host Protocol v1. Python, Go, Rust, or TypeScript callers send the stable ID and a JSON `Spec` object; the author-facing generic signature is descriptive metadata, not protocol identity. The same invocation can deterministically emit formed STEP, flat STEP, and SVG.

## Where to stop

Move the problem to C# when it needs database access, catalog search, joins, algorithms, external I/O, unbounded iteration, optimization, or large strategy search. Templates should make engineering families legible, not make the compiler clever.

docs/public/firmament/templates.md.title: Templates: typed engineering specialization
docs/public/firmament/templates.md.markdown:
# Templates: typed engineering specialization

Firmament Templates do not render text, documents, web pages, or source files. They specialize typed engineering models at compile time.

The useful mental model is generic engineering programming: one finite definition accepts typed parameters, checks admissibility, and becomes an ordinary concrete Firmament declaration before geometry or another domain artifact is materialized. Firmament borrows that mental category from C++ templates, but intentionally omits arbitrary recursive metaprogramming, macros, open-ended algorithms, and C++-style instantiation machinery.

## Canonical syntax

Angle brackets are mandatory in canonical V2 source. A product-family Template declares parameters before its output declaration:

```firmament
Template<Width: Length, Height: Length, Thickness: Length>
Struct MountingPlate {
    Require Positive => Width > 0mm && Height > 0mm && Thickness > 0mm
    Box Plate { Size: [Width, Height, Thickness] }
}

Struct StandardPlate = MountingPlate<Width: 80mm, Height: 50mm, Thickness: 8mm>
```

The complete build-qualified version is [`generic-mounting-plate.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/generic-mounting-plate.firmament).

The explicit output keyword is significant: current Templates specialize `Struct`, `Model`, `Concept Struct`, `Panel`, `SheetMetal`, `Profile`, `ProfileDelta`, or module-owned `Subassembly` declarations. It is not inferred from the body.

A typed Subassembly export is specialized through an Inventory occurrence:

```firmament
Template<config: CylinderConfig>
Subassembly CylinderUnit {
  // Local Concept layout, Parts, Interfaces, Mates and public ports.
}
```

This is a definition fragment. Its consuming project supplies `CylinderConfig`
and instantiates `Units.cylinder<config: config>` through an Assembly occurrence;
see [Inventory](inventory.md). The existing one-parameter legacy Assembly Template
form remains compatible. This pass does not broaden it into a new generic syntax.

Product Template names have lexical scope. A Model-local definition shadows a
document definition, sibling scopes remain private, and duplicate names in one
scope reject. Nested applications resolve where the Template was defined.
Host metadata and host invocation expose document-level product Templates, or
Templates in the single Model used as a module container by existing libraries.
They do not merge private definitions from sibling Models.
Record, Static and Table declarations now use the same lexical ownership. A local
Record shadows its enclosing name while retaining a distinct nominal type;
sibling-private data is invisible. Defaults resolve in the definition scope and
explicit arguments in the caller scope. The geometry operations remain unchanged.

A finite feature Template used by `Pattern ... Over` has the same generic visual form:

```text
Template<spec: MountSpec> MountHole {
    Hole<Shaft> Mount {
        On: +Z
        Center: spec.Center
        Diameter: spec.Diameter
        End: ThroughAll
    }
}

Pattern MountPattern Over Mounts { MountHole<Current> }
```

The older `Template MountHole(MountSpec spec)` and `MountHole(Current)` spellings remain warning-free compatibility aliases. Current docs, fixtures, and snippets use angle brackets.

`Template<>` is valid. It exists for uniform specialization and compatibility, but a declaration with no variable engineering input is usually clearer as an ordinary `Struct`.

## Parameters

`Options` and `Enum` define the same finite nominal choice type. Preferred
`match` selects one result; legacy `Match` remains accepted. Every Enum case,
or both Bool cases, must occur exactly once, and all arms must bind names and
produce the same type before selection. Unknown, duplicate and missing cases
reject even in an unselected arm. Only the selected value is evaluated.

A typed choice may travel through a scalar Static, a Record, a Template parameter
or default, and a Feature parameter or local. Record results must retain the same
nominal Record type; identical fields do not make unrelated Records interchangeable.
Arms may be separated by newlines or semicolons. Toleranced selections preserve
the selected requirement's allowance and provenance through the existing typed
transport; PMI still requires an explicit projection.

```firmament
Options PlateSize { Compact Standard }
Template<size: PlateSize = Standard,
         width: Length = match size { Compact => 40mm; Standard => 80mm }>
Struct PlateFamily {
    Box stock { size: [width, 20mm, 5mm] }
}
Struct Plate = PlateFamily<size: Compact>
```

`Set<T>` contains all entries at once for Pattern; it does not replace choices.
See the working
[`table-driven-mounting-plate.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/table-driven-mounting-plate.firmament)
for enum-valued Record data, and [Writing Firmament](../reference/language/data-and-choices.md#choices-options-and-match)
for the expression contract and the bounded legacy numeric Pattern-source selector.
A match expression does not execute arbitrary declaration blocks or admit new
geometry capabilities. Static Enum values use an explicit nominal type annotation,
such as `Static size: PlateSize = Compact`.

Scalar `Static` bindings and typed Record fields can carry
[typed tolerances](pmi.md#project-a-compile-time-tolerance). Scalar or whole-Record
Template arguments preserve nominal value, dimensional type, allowance and
original-source provenance through nested specialization. Checked `with`
overrides replace individual requirements. Scalar defaults use the same typed
value binder. Features can accept either the scalar field or the whole typed
Record; direct local aliases retain the allowance. Arithmetic retains the
documented nominal-only policy and warns when it drops an allowance.
This does not grant arbitrary scalar environments to every material domain or
implement tolerance-stack arithmetic. See the complete
[Record/Template/Feature example](../reference/language/requirements.md#tolerances).

Value parameters use `Name: Type`. Defaults use `Name: Type = Value`. A real semantic/type parameter is explicit:

```text
Template<type TBody satisfies PrismaticBody, Width: Length, Variant: BracketVariant = Standard>
Struct BracketFamily {
    // existing construction
}
```

`type TBody satisfies PrismaticBody` is not an ordinary string-valued choice. The binder verifies that the supplied declaration satisfies the named language `Concept`. All other current parameters are typed compile-time values.

| Parameter kind | Preview 3 | Declaration | Checking and defaults | Forge.Host |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Length` | Supported | `Width: Length` | `mm`; defaults supported | dimension `length`, unit `mm` |
| `Angle` | Supported | `Draft: Angle` | `deg`; defaults supported | dimension `angle`, unit `deg` |
| integer | Supported | `Count: Int` | integer literal; defaults supported; lowercase alias accepted | JSON integer |
| number | Supported | `Ratio: Float` | finite numeric literal; defaults supported; lowercase alias accepted | JSON number |
| boolean | Supported | `Enabled: Bool` | `true` / `false`; defaults supported; lowercase alias accepted | JSON boolean |
| string | Supported | `Label: String` | quoted literal; defaults supported | JSON string |
| enum choice | Supported | `Variant: BracketVariant` | declared cases; defaults supported | allowed values listed |
| `Record` | Supported | `Spec: BracketSpec` | immutable `Static` value; nested fields checked | JSON object and field schema |
| `ImportedStep` | Supported at host seam | `Source: ImportedStep` | typed host resource token | transported as a host resource |
| `ProfilePath` | Supported in the profile-delta lane | `Owner: ProfilePath` | qualified semantic path | typed string boundary |
| semantic/type parameter | Supported | `type T satisfies Concept` | language Concept conformance; no default | category and constraint exposed |
| material reference | Not a distinct Template type | use a supported semantic material identity in the consuming domain | resolution stays in Firmament/Forge/C# | no catalog query surface |
| arrays/lists | Not a direct product-Template parameter | consume finite `Static` arrays through feature Templates/Patterns | element Record checked | not exposed as a parameter |
| `Table` | Not a direct parameter | select a row into a `Static Record` first | key and row checked | selected Record can cross the host seam |
| `Force` and other quantities | Not supported by the generic binder | — | `Length` and `Angle` are the admitted dimensions | — |
| `Profile`, feature kind, or Template | Not supported as generic parameters | — | no higher-order Templates | — |

This matrix describes the compiler today. It is not a roadmap.

## Records, `with`, Static, Tables, and Patterns

`Record` defines grouped engineering-data shape. `Static` binds immutable compile-time data. `with` derives a new Record value by replacing checked fields; it is neither inheritance nor mutation. A keyed `Static Table` is finite engineering data, and a Table lookup produces a Record that can be passed to a Template. `Set<T>` is the source-ordered named form for finite immutable data; arrays remain the anonymous form. `Pattern ... Over` expands either compatible source through the existing finite semantic feature route.

```text
Record EnclosureSpec {
    Width: Length
    Height: Length
    WallThickness: Length
}

Static Desktop: EnclosureSpec = EnclosureSpec {
    Width: 180mm
    Height: 60mm
    WallThickness: 1.5mm
}

Static Rugged = Desktop with {
    WallThickness: 2mm
}
```

The coherent flow is: Records, Static values, and Tables define finite data; `with` derives configurations; a Template specializes from them; `Require` rejects inadmissible combinations; Pattern expands finite features; the resulting ordinary declaration follows the normal compiler and materializer path.

## Concepts and Require

A language `Concept` names a compile-time requirement. Structural Concepts specify
typed members and can compose other contracts. Predicate Concepts return Bool;
record-shaped requirement bundles label several predicates and require every
field to pass. `Concept Struct` is a non-materialized construction value that can
provide a structural contract. These differ from Forge C# runtime concept
descriptors, even though both carry engineering semantics.

Parameter types own structural and dimensional checking. Records own grouped data shape. Concepts own semantic conformance. `Require Name => BooleanExpression` owns specialization-specific admissibility. A failed `Require` stops specialization before geometry materialization and records the named check in specialization provenance.

Use `Require dimensions => PlateRequirements(width, height)` to apply a predicate
or bundle after argument binding. The same Boolean requirement syntax works in a
native mechanical Model. Comparisons, bounded Boolean combinations and dimensional
arithmetic use the shared AST; unapplied definitions are checked for type errors.
See the complete [requirement and bundle example](../reference/language/requirements.md#conditions-concept-and-require).
This is not a runtime script or a general constraint solver. Scalar inputs retain
their dimensional type; tolerances contribute nominal values rather than an
interval proof. Record fields can supply scalar arguments; whole Record and shape
predicate parameters are not admitted.

The established `Require Name { Actual: ... Expected: ... Tolerance: ... }` is a
different, domain-owned dimensional constraint used by projected PMI. It retains
its existing checking and projection path; it is not reinterpreted as a predicate
bundle. See [PMI](pmi.md).

## DFM policy families

An LLM-friendly DFM family has four ordinary pieces: a named policy `Concept`, a typed policy `Record`, one immutable `Static` default plus optional `with` variants, and a product `Template<Policy: ...>` that materializes one policy `Concept Struct`. The LLM normally changes only the Static data or selects a derived policy.

Canonical policy contracts are `CncManufacturingPolicy`, `FdmManufacturingPolicy`, `AdditiveManufacturingPolicy`, and `SheetMetalManufacturingPolicy`. The CNC and additive contracts are consumed by the existing DFM enforcement paths. CNC Pocket policy precedence is explicit: a Pocket-local `MinimumFloorThickness` wins, then the canonical CNC policy's floor value, then its wall value. FDM and sheet-metal policy structs are typed portable family data for their consuming domains.

Copy-ready, CLI-validated ports of the historical policy examples are:

- [`cnc-dfm-policy.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/cnc-dfm-policy.firmament)
- [`fdm-dfm-policy.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/fdm-dfm-policy.firmament)
- [`sheet-metal-dfm-policy.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Templates/sheet-metal-dfm-policy.firmament)

Persisted lowercase `template<CNC>`, `template<FDM>`, `template<Additive>`, and `template<SheetMetal>` sources remain compatibility inputs. When a canonical typed policy is present it is authoritative; new source should not emit the lowercase form.

## Termination and composition

Templates may not recursively specialize themselves, directly or through a cycle. Nested specialization is only useful when it is acyclic and lowers to the admitted concrete declarations; Templates are not first-class values, cannot be passed as parameters, and have no higher-order or recursive programming surface.

The practical complexity ceiling is deliberate:

- Use Firmament for finite declarative product families, typed configuration, dimensional checks, bounded semantic choice, and deterministic repetition.
- Use C# or Forge for algorithms, external I/O, material-database queries, joins/grouping, large search or optimization, and open-ended computation.

Firmament has no `Select`, `Where`, `GroupBy`, joins, query comprehensions, SQL surface, or arbitrary source generation. C# stays C#.

## Output boundary

The modern generic specializer admits `Struct`, `Model`, `Concept Struct`, `Panel`, `SheetMetal`, `Profile`, and `ProfileDelta` output declarations. Finite feature Templates admit the currently documented `Hole<Shaft>`, capsule/rounded-rectangle `Slot`, `Profile`, and `StandardPart` outputs. Templates can thereby influence existing geometry, Sheet Metal, semantic PMI inputs, and an Analysis contained in an admitted concrete model, but Preview 3 has no separate generic FEA or Drawing output contract and no new PMI feature kinds.

`Struct`, `Compose`, and `Modify` keep their ordinary meanings after specialization: `Struct` owns construction intent, `Compose` creates an admitted profile-based body, and `Modify` applies admitted post-construction semantic features. Template is not a geometry subsystem.

## Forge.Host

Protocol v1 keeps stable IDs such as `Standard.SheetMetal.ElectronicsEnclosure` separate from display signatures such as `ElectronicsEnclosure<Spec: EnclosureSpec>`. `ListTemplates` discovers stable IDs. `DescribeTemplate` exposes the signature, output kind, parameter category, units/dimensions, required/default state, enum cases, nested Record fields, named `Require` constraints, documentation, and artifacts. `InvokeTemplate` binds language-neutral values and returns deterministic artifacts and specialization identity; it never exposes compiler AST nodes.

Syntax cleanup therefore does not rename a public Template. See [Template engineering examples](template-examples.md) and the [Forge Host guide](../forge/interop.md).

Generic Profile output and bounded Point3 parameters are demonstrated in [source-owned guitar authoring](source-owned-guitar-authoring.md). Local guide names are specialization-owned; semantic Loop spans are preserved. Profiles are not higher-order Template arguments.

docs/public/firmament/threads.md.title: Bounded external threads
docs/public/firmament/threads.md.markdown:
# Bounded external threads

The external `Thread` feature cuts a finite groove into continuous major-diameter cylindrical stock. It supports the existing metric 60-degree truncated profile on a Cylinder or standalone HexBolt shank. The helical law, certified spline realization, and seam topology remain BRep authority.

`StartOffset` positions the groove centerline relative to the exposed cylindrical support start. `Length` sets its finite axial span; the bounded implementation admits 1–40 complete turns. The groove's outer footprint extends `7 * Pitch / 16` beyond each centerline endpoint. Leave stock outside that footprint at both ends. A HexBolt's support starts after `UnderHeadRadius` and ends before `TipChamferLength`. Invalid margins produce `thread-support-bounds` rather than clipping a thread into the head or chamfer.

The canonical Preview 4 witness is [hexbolt-showcase.firmament](../../../fixtures/Thread/hexbolt-showcase.firmament). Its 52 mm stock preserves 38 turns at 1.25 mm pitch, with 0.953125 mm of head-side land and 1.315625 mm of tip-side land. No tapered manufacturing runout is modeled.

```firmament
Thread MainThread {
    Surface: face(Bolt.Shank)
    MajorDiameter: 8mm
    Pitch: 1.25mm
    Length: 47.5mm
    StartOffset: 1.5mm
}
```

A standalone HexBolt may author `MakerMark`, `MakerMarkHeight`, and `MakerMarkDepth` together. Height and depth require explicit positive millimetres; the existing bounded planar cap engraving admits depth up to 0.3 mm. For example, `MakerMark: "CODEX"`, `MakerMarkHeight: 2.5mm`, `MakerMarkDepth: 0.2mm` reuse the established text profiles and counter handling. Reusable assembly engraving is explicitly unsupported. The old `ThreadedHexBoltMakerMark` C# entry point is deprecated.

Build through the repository CLI:

```powershell
dotnet Aetheris.CLI/bin/Release/net10.0/aetheris.dll build fixtures/Thread/hexbolt-showcase.firmament --output artifacts/local/p4-01b/showcase/bolt-cli.step --json
```

docs/public/firmament/viewport-themes.md.markdown:
# Telos viewport themes

Use **THEME** in Cadmata's viewport toolbar. The choice is remembered locally; `?theme=aurora` (or another theme ID) also selects a theme when opening Cadmata. Switching themes keeps the current camera, geometry, source identities and inspection selection.

| Theme | Treatment | Best use |
|---|---|---|
| Atelier | Graphite desk, neutral metal, balanced task lighting | General engineering work |
| Monument | Warm paper, clay surfaces, soft gallery lighting | Form, architecture and light-background screenshots |
| Blueprint | Cobalt drafting desk, porcelain blue surfaces, measured cyan grid | Topology and trim inspection |
| Mars | Amber low sun, copper strata, oxidized metal | Dramatic warm presentation |
| Sirius | Blue-white star, spectral halo, cold polished hardware | Cool hardware presentation |
| Singularity | Off-centre accretion rings, black stage, ember rim | High-contrast presentation |
| Aeons | Violet observatory, engraved gold arcs, antique metal | Quiet cosmic presentation |
| Aurora | Mint curtains, violet fill, titanium highlights | Colourful presentation |

All eight are static, on-demand WebGPU presentations. There is no continuous animation loop for decoration. Native standalone WGSL supplies one fullscreen backdrop pass; the existing Telos color/depth attachments still own the frame. Mesh lighting includes key/fill directions, hemisphere light, a roughness-dependent highlight, a coloured silhouette rim and tone mapping. It is an artistic lighting approximation, not an environment-map PBR renderer or a physical lighting simulation. Glow is drawn in the procedural background; no HDR bloom, shadow-map or fog postprocessing is claimed.

Minor and major grid lines follow the product palette and retain physical world spacing. The grid is a reference overlay, not a new model boundary. **GRID** still toggles it; Singularity intentionally starts without it. Source BRep edges, selection accents, axes and annotation panels use their product theme colours. Imported standalone parts use the chosen display material; authored assembly material facts remain in the source packet. CIR/SDF fields retain their compiler-generated shading ABI and authored materials, while sharing the theme backdrop, grid and selection treatment. The new mesh lighting does not imply new field shader lighting support.

Helios retains its Mars/Sirius product choices and now projects both into the same native Telos presentation API. The WebGL fallback retains its older, simpler presentation; the eight-look qualification is for WebGPU.

For surface comparison, use [Surface and trim inspection](surface-inspection.md). Its wire and face-isolation modes remain available under every theme. Prefer Atelier, Monument or Blueprint when assessing small details; presentation themes intentionally use stronger colour contrast.

Reusable configuration lives in `@aetheris/three-telos`: `host.setPresentation(TelosPresentation)`. Product adapters project palette and light settings into that contract. Backdrop/grid colours are display encoded, lighting colours are linear. `setPresentation` resets temporal history after an appearance change, retains geometry and camera, and requests an on-demand frame. Each backdrop shares one pipeline per attachment/sample configuration; changing palette does not generate shader programs.

`scripts/qualify-viewport-themes.mts` records actual Cadmata uploads, matched-camera images, stable source-face clicks and bounded pipeline cycling. Supply the Playwright module, local McMaster directory, ignored output directory, host URL and specimen ID. Generated captures belong under `artifacts/local/viewport-themes/`.

docs/public/firmament/wire-form.md.title: Formed Wire
docs/public/firmament/wire-form.md.markdown:
# Formed Wire

Use `WireForm` when the design intent is a formed length of constant-section wire or rod. Authors specify the forming sequence; Aetheris derives the exact tangent centerline and materializes it with the circular Sweep kernel.

```firmament
WireForm BentWire {
    Diameter: 1mm
    Material: Standard.Materials.StainlessSteel.304_Annealed
    StartFrame { Origin: [0mm, 0mm, 0mm]; Tangent: [1, 0, 0]; Up: [0, 0, 1] }
    Straight Lead { Length: 20mm }
    Bend Corner { Radius: 5mm; Angle: 90deg; Plane: Up }
    Straight Tail { Length: 30mm }
}
```

Fields accept the canonical camelCase spelling (`diameter`, `material`, `radius`,
`turns`, `pitch`) and their established PascalCase aliases. Names and domain
symbols retain their authored case.

`Diameter` and `Material` define the stock. Direct WireForm authoring uses the catalog identity; a typed product policy may carry that identity through a `String` field. `StartFrame` supplies an origin, initial tangent, and perpendicular `Up` reference. A `Straight` advances along the current tangent and preserves the frame. A signed `Bend` rotates the tangent by `Angle` around either the current local `Up` or `Right` axis. Here `Plane` names the current local **plane normal/rotation axis**: `Plane: Up` bends in the tangent/right plane, while `Plane: Right` bends in the tangent/up plane. The frame is transported by the same rigid rotation, avoiding arbitrary spin. Start-frame transformations therefore carry the forming program without global-coordinate bend hacks.

`Radius` is always the **centerline bend radius**. Wire forming applies a geometric-only minimum-radius rule: `Radius > Diameter / 2`. It does not invent material forming tables. Positive angles follow the right-hand rule about the selected local plane normal; negative angles reverse that normal. X0 admits nonzero angles through ±180°.

Each operation consumes a `WireState` (position, tangent, local frame, and accumulated length) and produces the next state. Changing an operation intentionally moves every downstream operation. The compiler retains operation identity and exposes the operation-to-line/arc-to-cylinder/torus correspondence through structured inspection.

The ideal cut-stock length is derived exactly:

- Straight: `Length`
- Bend: `Radius × abs(AngleRadians)`
- Total: the sum of all operation lengths

Circular area times total length gives volume; density from the Material DB gives mass. These are idealized centerline quantities. It does not model springback, plastic stretch, forming allowance corrections, or manufacturing process simulation.

The centerline lowers to explicit line and circular-arc AIR, then to exact circular Sweep geometry. Straights become cylinders, bends become toroidal patches, and open terminals become planar caps. Canonical WireForms have no rational B-spline surfaces and no faceted fallback. Both terminals retain position, tangent/frame, and section diameter.

STEP export retains these analytic surfaces and circular edge bases. Face boundaries follow their outward normals, so a downstream CAD reader receives the intended bend side without needing to repair the wire's winding.
When STEP edges lack surface-parameter trims, import derives exact linear trims for cylinder generators and rings, and torus major and minor circles. Straight/Bend wire forms do not need fitted B-spline trim curves; seam boundaries retain their full angular spans. Existing source trim curves are preserved rather than rewritten.

Winding generators extend wire forming without weakening the exact Straight/Bend route. `Helix` authors a cylindrical helix from `Radius`, `Turns`, either `Pitch` or `Height`, explicit `Handedness`, and an optional stable `StartPhase`. If both Pitch and Height are supplied they must agree with `Height = Turns × Pitch`. The compiler derives the missing value, exact helix length, terminal position/tangent/transported frame, turn clearance, volume, and mass. `AxisCoil` remains accepted as a compatibility spelling and lowers to the same semantic operation. The axis is derived from the current wire state rather than specified as an independent field.

```firmament
Helix Winding {
    Radius: 12mm
    Turns: 8
    Pitch: 5mm
    Handedness: RightHanded
    StartPhase: 0deg
}
```

`SurfaceCoil` has an evaluable centerline law for analytic `Cylinder`,
`Frustum`/`Cone`, and `Sphere` supports. This is currently **internal centerline
qualification**, not an admitted multi-body Model recipe. Declaring support
solids alongside a WireForm fails normal validate/build admission; the compiler
does not silently discard those solids. An explicit nonmaterial support binding
is still needed. The preserved [regression witnesses](../../../fixtures/Regression/WireFormSurfaceSupport/README.md)
record the boundary. Cylinder/frustum winding uses `AxialPitch`. Sphere winding
uses linear-latitude progression between `StartLatitude` and `EndLatitude`,
without equal-geodesic-spacing claims and excluding the exact poles.

**Internal centerline fragment — this is not a complete buildable Model:**

```firmament
Frustum CupInnerFrustum { BottomRadius: 18mm; TopRadius: 30mm; Height: 60mm }
SurfaceCoil Winding {
    Surface: CupInnerFrustum
    Side: Inside
    Clearance: 1mm
    Turns: 6
    AxialPitch: 8mm
    Handedness: RightHanded
}
```

`Clearance` is support-to-wire clearance; the compiler uses `Diameter / 2 + Clearance` as centerline offset. `CenterlineOffset` is the mutually exclusive mathematical alternative. Collapsing inward offsets, pole singularities, turn overlap, and unsupported surfaces fail with typed diagnostics. CLI inspection reports the winding kind/law, handedness, resolved pitch/height, exact or deterministically integrated stock length, start/end terminals, self/support clearance, and polynomial realization evidence.

The semantic/evaluable winding law remains authoritative. Coil-containing forms lower through deterministic rotation-minimal frame transport to cubic non-rational B-spline tube patches and planar caps; STEP uses no rational product surfaces and no faceted fallback. Coil-free forms still use exact cylinders and tori. The current approximation uses 32 longitudinal cubic spans per turn and four cubic polynomial quarter patches around the circular section; the compiler measures maximum/RMS centerline error against the winding law and fails if its 0.01 mm bound is exceeded.

Coils remain continuous, unbranched, open paths. A distinct closed `Knot` operation for named mathematical knot families; it does not turn coils into closed paths or force Straight/Bend through spline approximation. See [Mathematical Knots](mathematical-knots.md). Arbitrary/freeform supports, variable pitch or section, intentional contact, spring mechanics, contact dynamics, and branching remain unsupported. Surface support identity is authored rather than imported-face-ID based. Direct `Concept Path` plus `Sweep` remains the lower-level choice for explicitly authored line/arc trajectories.

See the canonical [Helix](../../../fixtures/Canonical/WireForm/helix.firmament),
[AxisCoil compatibility fixture](../../../fixtures/Canonical/WireForm/axis-coil.firmament),
[composed Straight/Coil/Straight](../../../fixtures/Canonical/WireForm/straight-coil-straight.firmament),
[90-degree bend](../../../fixtures/Canonical/WireForm/single-bend-90.firmament),
and [Paperclip](../../../fixtures/Canonical/WireForm/paperclip.firmament).

`aetheris inspect source.firmament --json` reports the semantic `wireForm` object, including `operations`, `totalStraightLength`, `totalBendLength`, and compiler-derived `totalWireLength`. A materializing `build --json` adds volume, mass, surface inventory, manifold/reimport status, rational/faceted counts, and the STEP hash.

The [single-cut guitar witness](../demos/guitar-surfacing-x0.md) reuses this exact Straight/Bend route for six thin strings. Each speaking length and tuner lead meets through a 3 mm centerline-radius bend at the nut. This is geometric routing, without string tension, vibration, wound-wire microgeometry, or tuner mechanics. Adjacent-operation clearance samples straight and curved operations on the same arclength interval count before excluding the intended tangent-join neighborhood.

## Mating a coil to a rod

A `Helix` starts at the current wire point and preserves its tangent. Its winding axis is generally **offset from that point and tilted from StartFrame.Up**: pitch contributes an axial component to the tangent. Do not mate the part origin or assume local Z is the spring axis.

Executable Assembly template occurrences expose each `Helix` operation by its authored name. For `Helix Winding`, the public semantic members are `Winding.Axis`, `Winding.Frame` and `Winding.ClearDiameter`. They come from the same compiler-derived axis origin, direction, start radial and wire radius that build the coil. The frame's Z axis is the winding axis, X is its start radial, and its origin is the winding-axis base. Clear diameter is twice the coil centerline radius minus wire diameter. The build report retains these values as `wireForm.operations[].axisDatum`.

A bounded spring-to-rod interface can combine axial alignment with a seating frame:

```firmament
Interface SpringOnRod {
    Role Spring requires AxisCapable, DatumFrameCapable, DimensionalCapable;
    Role Rod requires AxisCapable, DatumFrameCapable, DimensionalCapable;
    Lower AxisCoincident Spring.Axis Rod.Axis;
    Lower FrameCoincident Spring.Frame Rod.Frame SameDirection;
    Fit Rod.Diameter inside Spring.ClearDiameter;
}
```

The datum frame fixes axial seat position and roll; the explicit axis constraint independently validates coaxiality after materialization. Fit analysis classifies diameter compatibility. See the executable [coil-on-stem fixture](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Assembly/coil-on-stem.firmament). This automatic datum exposure covers `Helix` and its `AxisCoil` compatibility spelling; it does not infer an axis for knots or arbitrary SurfaceCoil supports.

docs/public/forge/interop.md.title: Forge Host Protocol v1
docs/public/forge/interop.md.markdown:
# Forge Host Protocol v1

Forge interop has three operations: list Templates, describe one Template, and invoke it. The host owns Firmament types, units, defaults, `Require` checks, specialization, geometry, and artifact production. Foreign clients only exchange explicit JSON and files.

Forge Host also publishes `Standard.Products.Office.Paperclip`. `describe` exposes its `PaperclipPolicy` Record fields and metric units; `invoke` accepts those fields, lowers them to a semantic WireForm Straight/Bend sequence, and emits `paperclip.step` through deterministic analytic AP242.

C# can use the direct Forge API. Python, Go, Rust, and TypeScript/Node use the process protocol:

```powershell
$forgeHost = ".\forge-host\Aetheris.Forge.Host.exe"
& $forgeHost list
& $forgeHost describe Standard.SheetMetal.ElectronicsEnclosure
python .\samples\forge-interop-x1\python\client.py $forgeHost .\samples\forge-interop-x1\request.json .\out\forge-python
go run .\samples\forge-interop-x1\go\main.go $forgeHost .\samples\forge-interop-x1\request.json .\out\forge-go
rustc .\samples\forge-interop-x1\rust\client.rs -o .\out\forge-rust.exe
.\out\forge-rust.exe $forgeHost .\samples\forge-interop-x1\request.json .\out\forge-rust
node .\samples\forge-interop-x1\typescript\client.ts $forgeHost .\samples\forge-interop-x1\request.json .\out\forge-typescript
```

These commands run from the extracted `Aetheris-win-x64` directory and require no source checkout. Repository developers can publish the same host from `Aetheris.Forge.Host`; the released NativeAOT executable above is the qualified product path.

The process command is `invoke <stable-template-id> --request - --out <directory>`. A minimal Python client can send the Protocol v1 JSON envelope directly:

```python
import json
import subprocess

host = r".\forge-host\Aetheris.Forge.Host.exe"
request = {
    "protocolVersion": 1,
    "arguments": {
        "width": "120 mm",
        "height": "40 mm",
        "depth": "80 mm",
        "thickness": "1.5 mm",
        "lidLipHeight": "8 mm",
        "insideRadius": "2 mm",
        "kFactor": 0.42,
        "reliefPolicy": "Rectangular",
    },
    "artifacts": ["StepAp242", "FlatStep", "Svg"],
}
completed = subprocess.run(
    [host, "invoke", "Standard.SheetMetal.ElectronicsEnclosure", "--request", "-", "--out", r".\out\forge-python"],
    input=json.dumps(request), text=True, capture_output=True, check=True,
)
response = json.loads(completed.stdout)
assert response["success"]
```

`describe` is the authority for argument names, categories, units, required/default state, enum cases, nested Record fields, named constraints, output kind, and artifacts. The stable ID is the invocation identity; the human-readable generic signature is descriptive metadata. Protocol callers never send Firmament source or compiler AST nodes.

For record-valued parameters, omitting the whole parameter selects its default record. Supplying a record currently requires every field; it does not merge a partial object with that default. For example, an explicit Paperclip `P` must include `WireDiameter`, both leg lengths, both bend radii, and `Material`. Nested `required: false` and `default` metadata currently describe the default record projection, not partial-object acceptance; a partial `P` fails with `firmament-template-record-missing-field`.

The shared production request is [`request.json`](../../../samples/forge-interop-x1/request.json), and the tiny clients are under [`samples/forge-interop-x1`](../../../samples/forge-interop-x1). Protocol v1 is language-neutral. The shipped NativeAOT binary and release bundle are qualified only for `win-x64`; framework-dependent tests on other operating systems establish protocol logic, not release-binary qualification.

docs/public/getting-started.md.title: Getting Started
docs/public/getting-started.md.markdown:
# Getting Started

Start with a self-contained [bundle](release-bundle.md) for Windows x64, Linux x64 or macOS Apple Silicon. It includes the compiler, Cadmata viewer, examples and runtime. If you only need the CLI, install the .NET global tool with the .NET 10 SDK:

```powershell
dotnet tool install --global Aetheris.CLI --version 2.0.0
aetheris --help
```

In a bundle, run the commands below from the extracted directory and use `.\aetheris.exe` (Windows) or `./aetheris` (Linux/macOS) in place of `aetheris`. The bundle supplies the `fixtures` used below and Cadmata for the final `view` command. For a source checkout, replace `aetheris` with `dotnet run --project Aetheris.CLI -c Release --`.

## Build a first part

The qualified first part is [`hole-diameter-and-datum.firmament`](../../fixtures/Canonical/PMI/hole-diameter-and-datum.firmament). It is a nontrivial plate with a through hole, datum, and toleranced diameter.

```powershell
aetheris validate fixtures/Canonical/PMI/hole-diameter-and-datum.firmament --json
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/PMI/hole-diameter-and-datum.firmament --output artifacts/local/first-part.step --json
aetheris analyze artifacts/local/first-part.step --json
```

Normal `validate` checks syntax, binding, units, targets and capability admission, including the engineering preflight required by the domain. It can construct geometry in memory; it does not write a build artifact. A successful validation exits zero and reports `firmamentV2Validation.status: "valid"` with its validation level. `--parse-only` is a limited check and does not prove build admission. `build` writes the real geometry and AP242 artifact; its JSON includes `success`, output path, diagnostics, feature reports, and `pmiExportEvidence` describing what was actually emitted. `analyze` independently reinspects topology and semantic PMI.

Use `aetheris view ...` to open Firmament or STEP in Cadmata when using a bundle.

## Build the canonical ordinary-CAD example

[`machined-mounting-block.firmament`](../../fixtures/Canonical/Integration/machined-mounting-block.firmament) is the first serious example after the small plate. It combines a base, connected Boss, finite Pocket, shaft hole, two counterbores, perimeter EdgeFinish, and semantic PMI while remaining a single readable source file:

```powershell
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/Integration/machined-mounting-block.firmament --output artifacts/mounting-block.step --json
aetheris analyze artifacts/mounting-block.step --json
aetheris view artifacts/mounting-block.step
```

## Invoke a Template

[`record-array-hole-pattern.firmament`](../../fixtures/Canonical/Patterns/record-array-hole-pattern.firmament) demonstrates typed Records, a static array, a Template, and `Pattern ... Over`:

When the elements need stable semantic names, use [`mounting-points.firmament`](../../fixtures/Canonical/Set/mounting-points.firmament): `Set<Point2>` preserves authored names and order, `MountPoints.UpperRight` addresses one value, and Pattern maps the complete finite set into construction.

```powershell
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/Patterns/record-array-hole-pattern.firmament --output artifacts/pattern.step --json
```

## Next

Work through [Learn Firmament](learn/README.md) to write parts like these yourself, or browse the [guides](README.md#guides) for sheet metal, FEA, STEP import and the rest.

docs/public/learn/01-first-part.md.title: 1. A first part
docs/public/learn/01-first-part.md.markdown:
# 1. A first part

You will build a 80 × 50 × 8 mm plate with one 8 mm hole through the middle, then
use the CLI to check it, build it and look at what came out.

## The source

[`01-plate.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament):

```firmament
// Lesson 1: a plate with one through hole.
Model Plate {
  units: mm

  Box stock { size: [80mm, 50mm, 8mm] }

  Modify stock {
    Hole<Shaft> mount {
      on: +Z
      center: Point2(0mm, 0mm)
      diameter: 8mm
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }
}
```

Line by line:

- `Model Plate { ... }` declares one part named `Plate`. One file can hold one or
  more declarations; a standalone part is a `Model`.
- `units: mm` sets the part's length unit. You still write units on every value.
- `Box stock { size: [...] }` creates the material body and names it `stock`.
  A Box is centred on X and Y and sits on the XY plane, so this one runs from
  Z = 0 to Z = 8 mm.
- `Modify stock { ... }` applies features to that body.
- `Hole<Shaft> mount` is a plain drilled hole named `mount`. The `<Shaft>` part
  picks the hole variant; lesson 3 uses the others.
  - `on: +Z` drills from the top face downward.
  - `center` is a point on that face, in the face's own X/Y coordinates.
  - `end: ThroughAll` takes it all the way through.

Names matter. `stock` and `mount` show up in reports, in STEP and in later
references such as PMI. Pick names you would use when talking about the part.

## Validate

```sh
aetheris validate fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament
```

```text
Firmament V2 validation: valid (0 fatal, 0 warning)
```

`validate` parses the file, checks every name, field and unit, and confirms the
compiler can admit each request. Add `--json` for a machine-readable report.

To see what a mistake looks like, misspell `diameter` as `diamter` and validate
again:

```text
plate.firmament(11,7): fatal firmament-v2-canonical-field-unknown:Hole:diamter: Unknown field 'diamter' in Hole. Check this construct's documented fields.
```

Each diagnostic gives a file, line and column, a stable code you can search for,
and a message. The real error is usually the most specific one; here, the
unknown field. Summary diagnostics such as `firmament-v2-parse-failed` only tell
you that compilation stopped. See [diagnostics](../reference/diagnostics.md).

## Build

```sh
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament --output artifacts/local/plate.step
```

The output is an exact STEP AP242 file: six planar faces and one cylindrical
hole wall, with no triangles and no approximation. Any CAD tool that reads STEP
can open it. Add `--json` to get a build report listing the features that were
produced.

## Check what you built

```sh
aetheris measure fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament
```

```text
Volume: 31597.876140340508 mm^3; ... method=ExactRectangularStockMinusThroughHoles; errorBound=0 mm^3
Topology: 7 faces, 15 edges, 12 vertices, 1 shells
Assert Bounds stock { min: [-40mm, -25mm, 0mm]; max: [40mm, 25mm, 8mm]; tolerance: 0mm; }
```

`measure` builds the part and reports what it measured: volume, bounds and
topology, plus ready-to-paste `Assert` lines. Lesson 5 turns those into checks
that run on every build. To inspect a STEP file directly, from any source, use
`aetheris analyze artifacts/local/plate.step --json`.

With the Windows bundle, `aetheris view fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament`
opens the part in Cadmata.

## Try it

- Move the hole to `Point2(25mm, 10mm)` and rebuild.
- Change `end: ThroughAll` to `end: Blind 5mm` for a 5 mm deep blind hole.
  The [hole fixtures](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Features/Holes/) show every
  form.
- Make the hole 60 mm wide, wider than the plate, and read the diagnostic: the
  compiler refuses to cut the plate into two pieces rather than export something
  you did not ask for.

Next: [2. Profiles](02-profiles.md).

docs/public/learn/02-profiles.md.title: 2. Profiles
docs/public/learn/02-profiles.md.markdown:
# 2. Profiles

Most real parts are not boxes. The usual way to make one is to draw its outline
in 2D and give it thickness. In Firmament that takes three steps:

1. **Construction geometry**: points, lines, rectangles and circles that describe
   the shape. They are guides only and create no material.
2. **A Profile**: closed loops traced from those guides, with a definite inside
   and outside. Holes are inner loops.
3. **A material operation** such as `Extrude`, which turns the Profile into a
   solid.

There is no sketch solver. You state dimensions and positions directly, so the
shape is always exactly what the numbers say.

## The source

[`02-bracket-profile.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Learn/02-bracket-profile.firmament)
makes a flat L-shaped bracket with a mounting hole in its upright leg:

```firmament
// Lesson 2: draw a closed 2D boundary, then extrude it.
Model BracketPlate {
  units: mm

  // Construction geometry only: nothing here is material yet.
  Concept Struct layout on XY {
    Polygon2<Explicit> outline {
      points: [[0mm, 0mm], [60mm, 0mm], [60mm, 15mm], [15mm, 15mm], [15mm, 40mm], [0mm, 40mm]]
    }
    Circle2 bore { center: [7.5mm, 30mm]; diameter: 6mm }
  }

  // A Profile turns guides into closed loops with an inside and an outside.
  Profile section using layout {
    Loop Outer { outline |> TraceLoop }
    Loop Inner { bore |> TraceLoop }
  }

  // Extrude gives the Profile thickness, from Z = 0 to Z = 6mm.
  Extrude bracket { profile: section; from: 0mm; to: 6mm }
}
```

- `Concept Struct layout on XY` groups construction geometry on the XY plane.
  `Concept` marks it as design data: it never becomes material by itself.
- `Polygon2<Explicit>` is a polygon from listed corner points. The compiler
  checks winding, repeated points, self-intersection and zero area.
- `Profile section using layout` reads guides from `layout`.
  `outline |> TraceLoop` copies a whole closed guide into a loop. The `Inner`
  loop becomes a hole through the part.
- `Extrude bracket` makes the solid. Its result is one body with nine faces: six
  sides, top, bottom and the bore wall.

## Simple shapes in one line

A rectangle, circle or slot can be a Profile directly:

```firmament
Profile stockOutline = Rect2 { center: [0mm, 0mm]; size: [70mm, 44mm] }
```

This uses the same exact boundary as the longer form. Lesson 3 uses it for every
outline.

## Tracing edge by edge

When a loop should follow selected edges, or you want to name the edges for
later reference, trace them in order with `|>`:

```firmament
Model ProfilePlate {
  units: mm
  Concept Struct layout on XY {
    Rect2 boundary { center: [0mm, 0mm]; size: [30mm, 24mm] }
  }
  Profile outline using layout {
    Loop Outer {
      boundary.Bottom as south
      |> boundary.Right as east
      |> boundary.Top as north
      |> boundary.Left as west
      |> Close
    }
  }
  Extrude stock { profile: outline; from: 0mm; to: 12mm }
}
```

Each stage continues from where the previous one ended; `as` names the resulting
edge, and `Close` checks that the loop really closes. It never adds a missing
segment for you. A gap or an ambiguous continuation is an error.

## Shapes you can use

| Shape | Main fields |
|---|---|
| `Rect2`, `Square2` | `center`, `size` |
| `RoundedRect2` | `center`, `size`, `radius` |
| `Circle2` | `center` and one of `radius` or `diameter` |
| `Ellipse2` | `center`, `axisLengths` (full lengths) |
| `Slot2` | `center`, `length` (overall, including both round ends), `width` |
| `Triangle2<...>` | `Equilateral`, `Isosceles`, `Right` or `Explicit` |
| `Polygon2<...>`, `RegularPolygon2<N>` | named polygon variants or an N-sided regular polygon |
| `Point2`, `Line2`, `CubicBezier2` | open guides for tracing |

The full field list is in [profiles and 2D construction](../reference/language/profiles.md).

## Other planes

Change `on XY` to `on XZ` or `on YZ` to draw on another principal plane. On XZ
the bracket stands upright and extrudes along −Y; try it and check the new
bounds with `aetheris analyze`.

## Try it

- Add a second `Circle2` and a second `Inner` loop.
- Replace the polygon with a `RoundedRect2` and compare the face count.
- Swap `[60mm, 0mm]` and `[60mm, 15mm]` so two edges cross, and read the
  `firmament-boundary2-explicit-self-intersection` diagnostic.

For curves defined by equations, revolved profiles and sweeps along a path, see
[equation curves](../firmament/equation-curves.md), [Revolve](../firmament/revolve.md)
and [Sweep](../firmament/sweep.md).

Next: [3. Features](03-features.md).

docs/public/learn/03-features.md.title: 3. Features
docs/public/learn/03-features.md.markdown:
# 3. Features

Machinists think in features: start from stock, raise a boss, mill a pocket,
drill and counterbore, break the edges. Firmament lets you write a part the same
way, and each feature keeps its name and meaning all the way into STEP.

## The source

[`03-machined-block.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Learn/03-machined-block.firmament):

```firmament
// Lesson 3: one body built from a stack of manufacturing features.
Model MachinedBlock {
  units: mm

  Profile stockOutline = Rect2 { center: [0mm, 0mm]; size: [70mm, 44mm] }
  Profile padOutline = Rect2 { center: [-16mm, 0mm]; size: [14mm, 14mm] }
  Profile recessOutline = Rect2 { center: [10mm, 0mm]; size: [20mm, 16mm] }

  Compose body {
    Base stock { profile: stockOutline; from: 0mm; to: 12mm; role: Stock }
    Boss pad { on: Top; profile: padOutline; height: 6mm }
    Pocket recess { on: Top; profile: recessOutline; depth: 4mm; minimumFloorThickness: 3mm }
    Hole<Shaft> bore { on: +Z; center: [-16mm, 0mm]; diameter: 6mm; end: ThroughAll }
    Hole<Counterbore> mountNorth {
      on: +Z
      center: [26mm, 13mm]
      diameter: 6mm
      counterboreDiameter: 11mm
      counterboreDepth: 3mm
      end: ThroughAll
    }
    Hole<Countersink> mountSouth {
      on: +Z
      center: [26mm, -13mm]
      diameter: 6mm
      countersinkDiameter: 12mm
      countersinkAngle: 90deg
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }

  Modify body {
    EdgeFinish<Chamfer> perimeterBreak {
      target: stockOutline.Outer
      on: Top
      distance: 1mm
    }
  }
}
```

## Compose

`Compose body { ... }` builds one body from an ordered list of operations.

| Operation | What it does | Key fields |
|---|---|---|
| `Base` | the starting stock, a Profile between two heights | `profile`, `from`, `to` |
| `Boss` | raised material on a support | `on`, `profile`, `height` |
| `Pocket` | a finite-depth recess | `on`, `profile`, `depth`, `minimumFloorThickness` |
| `Hole<Shaft>` | a drilled hole | `on`, `center`, `diameter`, `end` |
| `Hole<Counterbore>` | a hole with a flat-bottomed recess | adds `counterboreDiameter`, `counterboreDepth` |
| `Hole<Countersink>` | a hole with a conical entry | adds `countersinkDiameter`, `countersinkAngle` |

`on: Top` means "the current top of the material under this feature". The pad
sits on the 12 mm stock top, so it runs from Z = 12 mm to Z = 18 mm. Order
matters: each operation sees the result of the ones before it.

`minimumFloorThickness` is a manufacturing requirement, not geometry. If a later
change made the pocket floor thinner than 3 mm, the build would fail instead of
producing a fragile part.

A Pocket never goes through. For a through cut, use a `Hole`, a slot, or
`Pocket` with `end: ThroughAll`.

## Hole variants

The part in angle brackets picks the variant, and each variant accepts only its
own fields. A `counterboreDepth` on a `Hole<Shaft>` is an error, not something
silently ignored. That rule applies across the language: an unknown or
misplaced field always rejects.

## Edge finishes

`EdgeFinish<Chamfer>` and `EdgeFinish<Fillet>` break edges. Here
`target: stockOutline.Outer` with `on: Top` selects the whole top rim of the
stock profile. A chamfer takes `distance`, a fillet takes `radius`.

Edge finishing is where CAD kernels get hard, so Aetheris supports specific,
well-defined selections, such as a profile rim, a Box's top boundary or every
edge of a convex stock, and rejects the rest with a diagnostic. The
[fillet and chamfer guide](../firmament/fillet-profiles.md) lists what combines
with what.

## Look at the result

```sh
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/Learn/03-machined-block.firmament --output artifacts/local/block.step --json
```

The JSON `engineeringFeatures` list reports `Boss`, `Pocket` and `EdgeFinish`,
and `featureCount` is 6. That report is the compiler's account of what it
built, and every feature you wrote must appear in it. Run
`aetheris analyze artifacts/local/block.step --json` and look for
`"structuralAssessment": "enclosed-manifold"`: the STEP file reimports as one
closed solid.

## Try it

- Raise the pocket `depth` to 10 mm. That leaves a 2 mm floor, below the 3 mm
  you asked for, and the build fails with `firmament-pocket-minimum-floor-thickness`.
- Move `mountNorth` to `[12mm, 4mm]`, into the pocket, and read why its
  counterbore no longer has a flat face to sit on.
- Swap the chamfer for `EdgeFinish<Fillet>` with `radius: 1mm`. A fillet around a
  rim that already carries holes and a pocket is one of the combinations not
  supported yet, and the diagnostic says so instead of building a partial fillet.

Next: [4. Reuse](04-reuse.md).

docs/public/learn/04-reuse.md.title: 4. Reuse
docs/public/learn/04-reuse.md.markdown:
# 4. Reuse

Real products come in families: the same plate in three thicknesses, the same
bolt pattern on every bracket. Firmament handles this at compile time. You name
your data, write a recipe once, and specialize it. When the compiler finishes,
every value is fixed and every repetition is expanded. Nothing runs at build or
load time, and nothing in the STEP file depends on a script.

If you program, these analogies help:

| Firmament | Feels like | But |
|---|---|---|
| `Record` | a struct type | only data, no methods |
| `Static` | a `const` | evaluated once, at compile time |
| `with` | a copy with changes | the original never changes |
| `Feature` | a function | returns exactly one feature |
| `Set` + `Pattern` | a map over a list | always finite, every result keeps a name |
| `Template` | a generic type | specialized by the compiler, not at run time |
| `Concept` / `Require` | a static assertion | checked before any geometry is made |

There is no `for`, no `while`, no `if` statement and no mutable state.

## The source

[`04-plate-family.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Learn/04-plate-family.firmament):

```firmament
// Lesson 4: name the numbers, reuse the recipe, then specialize a family.
Record PlateSpec {
  width: Length
  depth: Length
  thickness: Length
  boltDiameter: Length
}

Static standard: PlateSpec = PlateSpec { width: 80mm depth: 50mm thickness: 8mm boltDiameter: 6mm }
Static heavy: PlateSpec = standard with { thickness: 12mm boltDiameter: 8mm }

Concept Positive(value: Length) => value > 0mm

Template<spec: PlateSpec> Model MountingPlate {
  units: mm

  Require positiveThickness => Positive(spec.thickness)
  Require boltsFit => spec.boltDiameter < spec.depth / 4

  // A Feature is a named, typed recipe. Calling it makes one hole.
  Feature Bolt(center: Point2, diameter: Length) -> Hole<Shaft> {
    return Hole<Shaft> {
      on: +Z
      center: center
      diameter: diameter
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }

  // A Set keeps every entry, by name and in order.
  Static corners: Set<Point2> {
    northEast => Point2(30mm, 15mm)
    northWest => Point2(-30mm, 15mm)
    southWest => Point2(-30mm, -15mm)
    southEast => Point2(30mm, -15mm)
  }

  Box stock { size: [spec.width, spec.depth, spec.thickness] }

  Modify stock {
    Pattern bolts over corners {
      corner => Bolt(center: corner, diameter: spec.boltDiameter)
    }
  }
}

Model StandardPlate = MountingPlate<spec: standard>
```

Reading from the top:

1. **`Record PlateSpec`** declares the shape of the data. Fields are typed:
   `Length` refuses an angle or a bare number.
2. **`Static standard`** is one value of that type. **`heavy`** derives a new
   value from it with `with`; `standard` itself is unchanged.
3. **`Concept Positive`** is a reusable yes/no check over compile-time values.
4. **`Template<spec: PlateSpec> Model MountingPlate`** is a part with a typed
   parameter. It is not built until something specializes it.
5. **`Require`** states conditions the parameters must meet. They are checked
   before any geometry exists.
6. **`Feature Bolt`** is the recipe for one hole.
7. **`Set<Point2>`** lists the bolt positions with names. `corners.northEast` is
   one of them.
8. **`Pattern bolts over corners`** applies the recipe to every entry, producing
   four holes named after their keys.
9. **`Model StandardPlate = MountingPlate<spec: standard>`** is the actual part.

Build it like any other part:

```sh
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/Learn/04-plate-family.firmament --output artifacts/local/plate-family.step
```

## Change one line

Specialize with `heavy` instead:

```firmament
Model StandardPlate = MountingPlate<spec: heavy>
```

`aetheris measure` now reports a 12 mm thick plate with 8 mm holes. Then set
`boltDiameter: 20mm` in `heavy` and validate:

```text
fatal firmament-template-require-failed:StandardPlate.boltsFit:20mm < 50mm / 4:...
```

The requirement names itself and shows the comparison that failed. No geometry
was attempted.

## Why named entries matter

Because each Set entry has a name, the four holes are `bolts.northEast`,
`bolts.northWest` and so on. If you insert a fifth position or reorder the list,
the existing holes keep their names, and so do PMI or other references that
point at them. Plain arrays are also available when order alone is enough; their
results are numbered by position instead.

## Choosing one option

To pick one of several values, declare the options and `match` on them:

```firmament
Model ConfiguredPlate {
  units: mm
  Options SizeChoice { Compact Standard }
  Static size: SizeChoice = Compact
  Static width: Length = match size {
    Compact => 40mm
    Standard => 80mm
  }
  Box stock { size: [width, 20mm, 5mm] }
}
```

Every option must be handled exactly once. There is no default arm, so adding a
new option is an error until you decide what it means everywhere it is used.

## Try it

- Add a fifth entry, `center => Point2(0mm, 0mm)`, to `corners`.
- Give `Bolt` a default: `diameter: Length = 6mm`, and drop the argument.
- Specialize a second part, `Model HeavyPlate = MountingPlate<spec: heavy>`, in
  its own file.

More: [Templates](../firmament/templates.md), [Patterns](../firmament/patterns.md)
and [compile-time data](../reference/language/data-and-choices.md).

Next: [5. Requirements and checks](05-requirements.md).

docs/public/learn/05-requirements.md.markdown:
# 5. Requirements and checks

A drawing says more than shape. It says which dimensions matter, how far they
may vary, and which faces everything is measured from. This lesson attaches that
information to the part and makes the build check its own output.

## The source

[`05-checked-plate.firmament`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Learn/05-checked-plate.firmament):

```firmament
// Lesson 5: state the requirement, publish it as PMI, and check the result.
Model CheckedPlate {
  units: mm

  Static boreDiameter: Length = 8mm tol +0.10mm -0.05mm

  Box stock { size: [40mm, 30mm, 8mm] }

  Modify stock {
    Hole<Shaft> bore {
      on: +Z
      center: Point2(0mm, 0mm)
      diameter: boreDiameter
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }

  // PMI travels with the STEP file as AP242 semantic annotation.
  Pmi {
    Datum A { target: face(+Z) }
    HoleDiameter boreSize { target: bore; dimension: boreDiameter }
  }

  // Assertions fail the build if the exported body is not what you meant.
  Assert Bounds stock {
    min: [-20mm, -15mm, 0mm]
    max: [20mm, 15mm, 8mm]
    tolerance: 0mm
  }
  Assert Topology stock { faces: 7; edges: 15; vertices: 12; shells: 1 }
}
```

Three separate ideas are at work here.

## 1. Tolerances are part of the value

`8mm tol +0.10mm -0.05mm` is a nominal 8 mm that may run 0.10 mm over or
0.05 mm under. `tol 0.1mm` alone means ±0.1 mm. Geometry is built at the
nominal size; the allowance travels with the value through Records, Template
parameters and Feature arguments.

Declaring a tolerance does not, by itself, put anything on a drawing, and it
never loosens the kernel's geometric precision. Arithmetic on a toleranced value
produces a plain nominal value and warns you, because the compiler cannot guess
what the combined tolerance should be.

## 2. PMI publishes requirements in STEP

The `Pmi` block chooses what to publish. `Datum A` marks the top face as a
reference. `HoleDiameter boreSize` attaches the bore's toleranced diameter to the
actual hole wall. Both are written as AP242 semantic PMI, so a downstream tool
reading the STEP sees a dimension tied to a face, not a picture of text.

`build --json` reports what was emitted under `pmiExportEvidence`: here one
datum and one diameter. A PMI request the exporter cannot represent is reported
as deferred rather than dropped. See [PMI](../firmament/pmi.md) for the
supported annotations.

## 3. Assertions check the result

`Assert` blocks describe the exported body: its bounds, its topology, or its
volume. `validate` and `build` both evaluate them, and a failed or unverifiable
assertion fails the build. Change `faces: 7` to `faces: 8` and build:

```text
fatal firmament-v2-assert-topology-failed: target=stock; Faces: expected=8, measured=7; ...
```

You rarely need to write assertions by hand. `aetheris measure` prints them for
the part as it is now; paste the ones that express your intent. Keep in mind
what each one protects:

| Assertion | Protects against | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `Assert Bounds` | the part moving or changing size | exact for supported stock shapes |
| `Assert Volume` | material quietly appearing or disappearing | uses an exact method or a guaranteed interval |
| `Assert Topology` | a feature being merged, split or skipped | counts faces, edges, vertices and shells |

Topology counts are strict, which is the point: if a chamfer stops being built,
the face count changes. Use them where the topology itself is the contract.

## Try it

- Run `aetheris build ... --json` and find `pmiExportEvidence` and
  `geometryAssertions` in the output.
- Change the bore to `tol 0.02mm` and rebuild. The geometry does not change; the
  published diameter does.
- Add `Assert Volume stock { expected: ...; tolerance: 0mm^3 }` using the value
  from `measure`.

More: [PMI](../firmament/pmi.md), [checks and measurement](../reference/language/checks.md).

Next: [6. Assemblies](06-assemblies.md).

# Learn Firmament

Six short lessons take you from an empty file to a checked, annotated part and a
two-part assembly. Each lesson builds one complete example, and every example is
a real file under [`fixtures/Canonical/Learn`](../../../fixtures/Canonical/Learn/)
that the test suite builds on every change. If a lesson's code is in this
repository, it compiles.

| Lesson | You will write | New ideas |
|---|---|---|
| [1. A first part](01-first-part.md) | a plate with a hole | `Model`, units, `Box`, `Modify`, `Hole`, the CLI loop |
| [2. Profiles](02-profiles.md) | an L-shaped bracket | construction geometry, `Profile`, loops, `Extrude` |
| [3. Features](03-features.md) | a machined block | `Compose`, `Boss`, `Pocket`, hole variants, `EdgeFinish` |
| [4. Reuse](04-reuse.md) | a family of mounting plates | `Record`, `Static`, `with`, `Feature`, `Set`, `Pattern`, `Template`, `Require` |
| [5. Requirements and checks](05-requirements.md) | a toleranced, self-checking plate | `tol`, `Pmi`, `Assert`, `measure` |
| [6. Assemblies](06-assemblies.md) | a post mounted on a plate | parts, published frames, `Interface<Fixed>` |

Before you start, install the CLI or use a source checkout, as described in
[Getting started](../getting-started.md). The commands below call it
`aetheris`. Run them from the repository root, or from the root of the extracted
Windows bundle, which ships the same `fixtures` folder.

## How to read Firmament

Firmament describes a finished object, not a sequence of commands. A file says
*what the part is*: this much stock, these holes, that chamfer. The compiler
works out the geometry, checks that every request was honoured, and writes exact
STEP AP242. If it cannot do what you asked, it stops and tells you why; it does
not quietly build something else.

Three habits will save you time:

1. **Write units on every length.** `8mm`, not `8`.
2. **Validate before you build.** `validate` is fast and points at the exact
   line that is wrong.
3. **Check the result, not just the exit code.** `measure` and `analyze` report
   what was actually built.

After lesson 6, the [language reference](../reference/language/README.md)
covers each construct in detail, and the [guides](../README.md#guides) cover
specific domains such as sheet metal, FEA and STEP import.

docs/public/project-boundaries.md.markdown:
# Geometry, field and display-compiler boundaries

`Aetheris.Kernel.Core` owns native geometry and BRep operations and has no project
or package dependency. `Aetheris.Fields` owns the analytic field expression tree,
deterministic evaluator tape, capability analysis and Visual TypeScript source
lowering. It depends only on Core. Both are AGPL-3.0-only libraries.

`Aetheris.Continuum` owns broader analysis, discretization and solver coordination.
It consumes Fields and retains the existing public field namespace and assembly
type forwarding. `Aetheris.Kernel.Firmament` owns authoring and display-artifact
coordination; its shader compiler is the pinned Copeland WGSL backend.

The current backend pin is `0.1.0-preview.1-a3.16c0ce996358af80`. Its seven NuGet
packages are Copeland.Markdown, Copeland.Profile, Copeland.SpanAllocation,
Copeland.TS, Copeland.TS.Mir, Copeland.TS.Workspace and Copeland.TS.Backend.Wgsl.
They are package dependencies for this downstream display path, not embedded
Copeland source projects or a dependency of native field evaluation. Building
the complete application restores them; packaging Fields/Core does not.

Consumers that need fields should reference `Aetheris.Fields`, not Continuum or
Firmament. See [fields](fields.md) for the package build, numerical admission and
source provenance contracts. GPU compilation remains the consuming renderer's
responsibility; Fields emits VTS source without depending on a shader compiler.

## Licence composition

Aetheris components retain AGPL-3.0-only. Copeland packages retain their own GPL
grants; no extraction here changes those licences. [GPLv3 section 13](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html#section13)
and [AGPLv3 section 13](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html#section13) allow
their combination. Each part retains its licence; corresponding-source and
notice requirements apply to conveyed combined builds, and AGPL's network-source
clause applies to the combination where its conditions are met.

Analytic shader implementation emitted from the field evaluator is conservatively
treated as AGPL-derived. Its provenance is retained with the generated source.
Artist assets and authored geometry descriptions retain their own terms; this
does not assert that all CAD exports acquire AGPL. A package/shader bake is not
a mechanism for silently removing the evaluator's licence boundary.

Aurelian's optional package adapter lives in Copeland at
`src/Integrations/Aurelian.Lighting.Aetheris`. Its own adapter/tracing source is
GPL, and the Aetheris dependency/emitted evaluator is AGPL. Aurelian's core does
not acquire a direct CAD project dependency. Existing humanoid and full bake
development bridges have separate, explicit source-checkout dependencies.

# Aetheris documentation

Aetheris is an exact, code-first CAD system. You describe a part, an assembly or
an analysis in **Firmament**, a small typed language, and the Aetheris compiler
turns it into exact STEP AP242 B-rep geometry, with its manufacturing intent and
PMI intact. When it cannot do exactly what you wrote, it stops and tells you why.

This folder is the user documentation and the authority on current behavior.
Everything else under `docs/` is development history, release records or legal
drafts; the [project history](../development/history/README.md) explains how the
system got here.

## Start here

1. [Getting started](getting-started.md): install the CLI and build a first part.
   With a release bundle, start from the [bundle walkthrough](release-bundle.md).
2. [Learn Firmament](learn/README.md): six short lessons, from a plate with a
   hole to a two-part assembly. Every example builds in CI.

   fields and its limits.

**If you are an AI agent writing Firmament**, read the lessons and the language
reference first, then the [modeling strategy skill](skills/firmament-modeling-strategy/SKILL.md)

docs/public/reference/3dm-recovery.md.title: 3DM geometry recovery evidence
docs/public/reference/3dm-recovery.md.markdown:
# 3DM geometry recovery evidence

3DM support is an optional tool because Rhino/OpenNURBS interoperability requires the native Rhino3dm library. Install it separately:

```powershell
dotnet tool install --global Aetheris.ThreeDm.CLI --prerelease
aetheris-3dm inspect model.3dm --json
aetheris-3dm recover model.3dm --json
```

The default `aetheris` compiler does not include Rhino3dm. Its old `inspect-3dm` / `recover-3dm` commands report how to install and invoke the companion tool.

From a source checkout, use `dotnet run --project Aetheris.ThreeDm.CLI -- inspect model.3dm --json` (or `recover`). Pack the optional tool with `dotnet pack Aetheris.ThreeDm.CLI -c Release -o artifacts/local/packages`; it is intentionally separate from `Aetheris.CLI`.

`aetheris-3dm inspect model.3dm --json` reads Rhino/OpenNURBS file metadata and BRep inventory. `aetheris-3dm recover model.3dm --json` measures bounded analytic and non-rational recovery candidates. Use `--body N --edge N` or `--body N --face N` with `recover-3dm` to inspect one source entity. `--recovery-tolerance-mm N` sets the generic spline budget (default 0.1 mm). The file's unit metadata determines conversion to Aetheris millimetres.

The recovery report is a **review aid**. It lists source object UUIDs, body/face/edge indices, degree and control-net sizes, candidate dimensions, RMS/p95/max deviations, angular deviations, rejected alternatives, and topology status. It also groups repeated radii as hypotheses. For unrecognized rational supports, `genericRecovery` reports the bounded non-rational candidate, its method, control-net complexity, and deviation against both the shared reducer and independent Rhino evaluation. The analysis mode does not build a BRep or STEP.

`aetheris-3dm recover model.3dm --bind-step --out-dir artifacts/local/3dm-bind --json` runs the separate topology-binding path. It preserves Rhino edge reuse, vertices, loops, and trim direction, retains source UV pcurves when qualified, and asks the shared recovered-pcurve binder for the rest. It exports only bodies that pass shell, pcurve, trusted STEP preflight, reimport, and sampled bounding-box checks. STEP files and the JSON report should stay under ignored `artifacts/local/` for private source models. Add `--body N` to bind just one source BRep.

Add `--combined-step` for a whole-file AP242 assembly when every source BRep qualifies. This emits `recovered-assembly.step` alongside deterministic per-object files; a source BRep with disconnected closed components contributes one STEP solid per component. Singular Rhino trims remain vertex semantics in the bound BRep. On mixed singular loops, the reference STEP omits pcurve associations that cannot yet roundtrip reliably, while preserving the 3D edges, faces, and source binding evidence. Explicit source vertex tolerances are capped locally at 1 mm and reported separately from the default 0.1 mm spline recovery budget. A near-coincident planar inner loop can be reimported under the explicit `AllowBoundedNearCoincidentInnerLoop` import policy; the default strict STEP importer continues to reject crossings.

Reported BRep bounds use 129 deterministic samples on each trimmed edge. Rhino's BRep bounding box can include the untrimmed support surfaces and substantially overstate a part's envelope. Edge-sampled bounds are useful for navigating this file but are not certified face-interior extrema.

Rational NURBS are source evidence. A simpler analytic carrier or non-rational spline may be proposed only with measured residuals and a stated qualification. A source geometric tolerance is not a manufacturing tolerance. Numerical agreement on sampled support geometry does not qualify face boundaries, edge uses, orientation, or shell enclosure. Production promotion needs those checks and an explicit caller policy. `TrustedProductionRoute` STEP export rejects rational B-spline surfaces and pcurves; legacy interchange output can retain them for compatibility and debugging.

The private Cartesian Product Design `.3dm` used in the [qualification work](../../development/history/eras/08-domain-expansion.md) is local-only and excluded from Git. Automation should keep detailed JSON under ignored `artifacts/local/`.
