docs/public/reference/language/README.md.markdown:
# Firmament language reference

This reference describes Firmament as the compiler accepts it today. It assumes
you have worked through the [lessons](../../learn/README.md), or at least read a
few complete examples. For a domain such as sheet metal or piping, the
[guides](../../README.md#guides) are the authority; they build on what is here.

| Page | Covers |
|---|---|
| This page | constructs at a glance, names and casing, values and units, layout |
| [Compile-time data and choices](data-and-choices.md) | `Record`, `Static`, `Table`, `with`, scope, `Options` and `match`, `Set` |
| [Requirements and interfaces](requirements.md) | `tol`, `Concept`, `Require`, `Semantic`, `Path` |
| [Profiles and 2D construction](profiles.md) | layouts, `Profile`, loops and `|>`, 2D shape families, frames and selectors |
| [Solids and features](solids-and-features.md) | primitives, `Modify`, `Compose`, holes, edge finishes, imported-geometry regions |
| [Reuse](reuse.md) | `Feature`, `Function`, `Pattern`, `Template`, mirror and radial symmetry |
| [Domains and modules](domains-and-modules.md) | `schema`, domain entry points, `BodyState`, `MeshState`, `Inventory`, `include` |
| [Assemblies and motion](assemblies-and-motion.md) | `Interface`, `Mate`, shared datums, joints, `Motion` |
| [Checks and measurement](checks.md) | `Assert`, `measure`, tolerance stack-ups, what `validate` and `build` check |
| [Reading older source](compatibility.md) | compatibility spellings and known inconsistencies |

## The rule that matters most

Firmament describes a finished artifact, and the compiler either produces what
you described or tells you why it cannot. An unknown field, an unresolved name,
an unsupported combination or a requirement that fails always rejects, with a
diagnostic pointing at the source. A successful build never means "built
something close". If you find a case where source is silently ignored, it is a
bug.

## Constructs at a glance

If you program, think of `Model` as a class that owns one artifact, `Struct` as
reusable construction, `Feature` as a typed function, and `Pattern` as a finite
loop. The analogies stop there: there is no inheritance, no runtime method, no
mutation and no general-purpose computation.

| Construct | What it describes |
| --- | --- |
| `Model` | A standalone part and its construction. |
| `Struct` | Named construction that a consuming artifact specializes or uses, such as an assembly part definition. |
| `Concept Struct` | Construction data that never becomes material: points, guides, frames, semantic members. |
| `Concept` | A compile-time requirement: a structural contract, a Boolean predicate, or a labelled bundle of predicates. |
| `Profile` | Named closed planar boundaries consumed by an extrusion or another feature. |
| `Feature` | A reusable recipe returning one typed result. |
| `Template` | Typed compile-time specialization of a product or bounded recipe. |
| `Record` / `Static` | A data shape / an immutable compile-time value. A Record is not a body. |
| `Options` (or `Enum`), `match` | A finite choice type, and exhaustive selection of one value. |
| `Set<T>` | Named entries of type `T`, available together for repetition. |
| `Semantic` | A named engineering interface: published datums, axes, points or dimensions. |
| `Path` | An ordered construction chain, open or closed. It creates no material. |
| `Pattern` | Finite repetition of construction over a declared source. |
| `Assembly` / `Scene` | Product occurrences and their relations / spatial composition and presentation. |

Use `Model` for an ordinary standalone part. A Struct, a Template library, a
Profile module and an Assembly each have their own entry and consumption rules;
they are not a Model with a different keyword.

## Declarations, fields and names

These are notation sketches, not complete files:

```text
Construct name { field: value }
Construct<Variant> name { field: value }
Feature Recipe(parameter: Type = defaultValue) -> ResultType { ... }
Struct instance = ProductFamily<parameter: value>
```

Braces delimit bodies, brackets delimit lists, parentheses delimit calls, and
`name.member` selects a published member. A colon labels a field, a parameter or
a declared type, depending on context. Declaration bodies, typed values and
Template specializations are distinct forms, not interchangeable object literals.

`<...>` means different things in different places: a built-in variant
(`Hole<Shaft>`), a collection element type (`Set<Point2>`), or Template
parameters and arguments. It does not make every construct generic.

Identifiers and published member names are case-sensitive. Preserve library
names exactly, including named call arguments: `spec.Width` does not become
`spec.width` because your local style is camelCase.

## Casing

| Role | Spelling | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Constructs and types | PascalCase | `Model`, `Box`, `Feature`, `Length`, `Point2` |
| Built-in fields | camelCase | `units`, `size`, `counterboreDepth` |
| Your geometry, values and parameters | camelCase | `stock`, `outline`, `mountPoint`, `depth` |
| Linking words | lowercase | `using`, `as`, `from`, `to`, `on`, `over`, `with`, `include`, `expose`, `bind`, `match` |
| Engineering symbols and enum values | as the domain spells them | `XY`, `+Z`, `Outer`, `ThroughAll`, `World`, `mm` |
| Geometry operations in pipelines | PascalCase | `Reverse`, `Close`, `TraceLoop` |

Most built-in fields also accept a PascalCase spelling (`Diameter` for
`diameter`), and older source uses it widely. New source should use camelCase.
For acronym fields write `pmi` and `bom`. This is not case-insensitive parsing:
the alias rule applies to built-in field names and linking words in their
admitted positions, never to your own names.

Some words appear both as a header clause and as a field.
`Concept Struct layout on XY` selects the plane of a layout; `on: +Z` inside a
Hole selects its support face. They are different positions with different
types. [Language style](../../firmament/language-style.md) describes what the
formatter changes, and the [cookbook](../../../../fixtures/Canonical/README.md)
shows the conventions applied across every canonical example.

## Values and units

Write units on every dimension in new source: `8mm`, `90deg`,
`Point2(12mm, -4mm)`. Bare numbers are for dimensionless counts and vector
components. `units: mm` belongs in an ordinary mechanical Model; it does not make
units optional in every field.

| Quantity | Units |
| --- | --- |
| `Length` | `mm` |
| `Angle` | `deg`; `rad` where a field documents it |
| `Time` | `s`, `ms` (motion only) |
| Volume (assertions) | `mm^3` |

Mixed degree/radian arithmetic needs an explicit conversion; the compiler will
not add the raw numbers. `Sin` and `Cos` take radians as a bare number, or an
angle with explicit units, and return a dimensionless value.

Planar points such as a Hole's or Rect2's `center` accept both `Point2(x, y)` and
`[x, y]`, with length coordinates. Arithmetic with dimensional checking is
available in admitted value positions, but not in every field of every domain;
the consuming guide says where.

For a hole on the top face of its host, `+Z`, `face(+Z)`, `Top` and `host.Top`
name the same support. The name of an unrelated body is not an alias for it.

## Layout, comments and terminators

Use two-space indentation. Put fields on separate lines, or separate them with
semicolons in a short body. Separate list elements and call arguments with
commas. Do not rely on the parser to split dense fields that run together.

Comments are `//` and `/* ... */`. `#` is not a comment marker.

A few specialized forms **require** semicolons: scalar `Function` expressions,
point-recipe fields, PMI `Note` fields and assembly root-provenance statements.
Their guides show them. There is no single statement-termination rule yet.

docs/public/reference/language/requireme.title: Requirements and interfaces
docs/public/reference/language/requireme.markdown:
# Requirements and interfaces

This page covers how a part states what must be true of it: dimensional
tolerances, compile-time conditions, structural contracts, and the named
engineering interfaces other parts and tools refer to.

## Tolerances

A tolerance is a requirement attached to a dimensional value:

```firmament
Model TolerancedPlate {
  units: mm
  Static drillDiameter: Length = 8mm tol +0.10mm -0.05mm
  Box Body { size: [40mm, 30mm, 8mm] }
  Modify Body {
    Hole<Shaft> Mount {
      on: +Z
      center: Point2(0mm, 0mm)
      diameter: drillDiameter
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }
  Pmi {
    HoleDiameter MountSize { target: Mount dimension: drillDiameter }
  }
}
```

- `tol 0.1mm` means ±0.1 mm. `tol +0.10mm -0.05mm` gives separate upper and
  lower allowances. Allowances are finite, non-negative, may be zero, and use the
  value's unit: mm for `Length`, deg for `Angle`. Tolerances on Int, Float, Bool
  or String reject.
- `tol` applies to the whole initializer, after any arithmetic.
- **Geometry uses the nominal value.** A tolerance never loosens the kernel's
  geometric precision.
- **Publishing is explicit.** Declaring a tolerance emits nothing by itself;
  `Pmi` projects it into AP242. See [PMI](../../firmament/pmi.md) for targets and
  export limits. Angle allowances can be bound and inspected, but angular PMI
  export from a Model is not supported yet.
- **Arithmetic drops allowances.** A direct alias keeps the tolerance. An
  arithmetic result is nominal, and the compiler warns that it dropped an
  allowance. If the result is a new requirement, give it its own `tol`. There is
  no inferred interval propagation and no tolerance-stack certification in
  scalar arithmetic; assembly stack-ups are a separate, explicit check (see
  [checks](checks.md#tolerance-stack-ups)).

Requirements travel through Records, Template parameters and Feature arguments
and locals:

```firmament
Record BoreSpec { diameter: Length }
Static production: BoreSpec { diameter: 8mm tol +0.10mm -0.05mm }

Template<spec: BoreSpec> Model PlateFamily {
  units: mm
  Feature Drill(spec: BoreSpec) -> Hole<Shaft> {
    let inspection: Length = spec.diameter
    return Hole<Shaft> {
      on: +Z
      center: Point2(0mm, 0mm)
      diameter: inspection
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }
  Box Body { size: [40mm, 30mm, 8mm] }
  Modify Body { Feature Mount = Drill(spec: spec) }
  Pmi { HoleDiameter MountSize { target: Mount dimension: spec.diameter } }
}
Model ProductionPlate = PlateFamily<spec: production>
```

Passing a scalar field or a whole Record keeps the requirement, as do nested
Records, `with` overrides, Template defaults and nested specialization. Feature
locals stay local: PMI in the enclosing Model names a Static or Record value it
can see. `validate --json` reports where each requirement came from and how it
was bound.

Where tolerances are not accepted:

- inline on a geometry field (`diameter: 8mm tol 0.1mm` rejects; name the value
  with a Static or Record field instead);
- in Table cells and other collection elements;
- in scalar positions of domains that take their inputs through typed Templates,
  such as Profile/Compose recipes, Sweep and WireForm. These reject unsupported
  scalar consumers rather than discarding the allowance.

## Conditions: `Concept` and `Require`

A predicate `Concept` is a named yes/no check over compile-time values. A
bundle `Concept` names several checks, each with a label. `Require` applies one:

```firmament
Concept Positive(value: Length) => value > 0mm

Concept PlateRequirements(width: Length, height: Length) {
  positiveWidth: Positive(width)
  positiveHeight: Positive(height)
  aspect: width >= height
}

Template<width: Length, height: Length> Model Plate {
  units: mm
  Require dimensions => PlateRequirements(width, height)
  Box Body { size: [width, height, 5mm] }
}
Model Product = Plate<width: 40mm, height: 20mm>
```

- Defining a Concept checks nothing; applying it does. `Concept AlwaysFalse => false`
  is legal until a `Require` uses it. Definitions are type-checked even when
  unused.
- `Require` works in Templates and directly in a mechanical Model with literal or
  Static inputs. It runs before any geometry is built.
- Predicate parameters are scalar `Length`, `Angle`, `Time`, `Int`, `Float`,
  `Bool` or `String`. Calls may be positional or named. Pass Record members, not
  whole Records.
- A bundle's labels name the failed check in the diagnostic, which beats a long
  chain of `&&`. `&&`, `||`, `!`, comparisons and dimensional arithmetic are all
  available, and every operand must resolve and type-check even if it would not
  change the answer.
- Zero-argument predicates can be referenced by name or called with `()`.
- Toleranced inputs are checked at their nominal values. This is not an interval
  proof.

Concepts are not runtime functions, do not convert units, cannot query arbitrary
geometry, and are not a constraint solver.

## Structural contracts

A structural `Concept` lists the typed members a construction must provide:

```firmament
Concept Bounded { Bounds: Box3 }
Concept Planar { TopPlane: Plane }
Concept PlateContract : Bounded && Planar { }
```

(These declarations are a fragment; a `Concept Struct` or Template uses them.)

Apply a contract with `type T satisfies PlateContract` or
`Concept Struct Design: PlateContract`. Conformance checks the members and their
types; a structural Concept is not a Boolean value. Composition with `&&` allows
identical inherited members and rejects conflicting types, duplicate own
members, missing contracts and cycles. A `Concept Struct` that claims a contract
publishes exactly that contract's members; to publish more, compose a larger
contract. There are no private members and no general inheritance.

Member names belong to you: `Bounds` is never silently renamed to `bounds`.
Concept names resolve within the part being compiled; there are no namespaces.

## Construction data: `Concept Struct`

`Concept Struct` holds design geometry that never becomes material, such as
layouts, guides and frames, or implements a structural contract. The `Concept`
prefix here is historical; it does not apply a predicate. Inside a layout, write
plain `Rect2`, `Circle2` and so on. Older spellings such as
`Concept Circle2 circle { ... }` bind to the same shapes with the same fields.

## Engineering interfaces: `Semantic`

`Semantic Name { ... }` groups references that consumers can name, such as a
mounting `DatumFrame` and a toleranced `Dimension`. It is usually published
through `expose`, or attached to an assembly occurrence. A Semantic is not a
second body, not a free-form metadata bag, and not a way to recognize arbitrary
BRep faces. Published values keep their types and source identity.

PMI selects which requirements to export; a Semantic alone exports nothing as
PMI. [Assembly authoring](../../firmament/assembly-authoring-foundation.md)
explains ports and placement.

## Paths

`Path` is an ordered chain of construction segments, open or closed. It creates
no material. An open Path can guide a Sweep; a Profile traced from a Path must be
closed. `Concept Path Name { ... }` is an older spelling of the same thing. See
[profiles](profiles.md).

docs/public/reference/language/reuse.md.title: Reuse
docs/public/reference/language/reuse.md.markdown:
# Reuse

`Feature`, `Function`, `Pattern`, `Template` and the symmetry operations let you
write construction once and use it many times. All of them are expanded by the
compiler into ordinary, finite construction. None of them adds mutable state,
exceptions, unbounded recursion, `for`/`while` loops or `if`/`else` statements.

## Feature: a typed recipe

A Feature definition describes one result; calling it produces that result where
it is called.

```text
Feature Drill(center: Point2, diameter: Length = 6mm) -> Hole<Shaft> {
  let depth: Length = diameter * 2
  return Hole<Shaft> { on: +Z; center: center; diameter: diameter; end: Blind depth }
}
```

- Parameters are typed, can be passed by position or by name, and can have
  defaults. Defaults may use other parameters, including dimensional
  arithmetic; cyclic defaults are errors.
- The body holds immutable `let` values and private construction, then exactly
  one `return`.
- A Feature may call another Feature with the same result type. Recursion is
  rejected.
- Result kinds include the Hole variants, `Boss`, `Pocket`, `EdgeFinish` and
  `Profile`. Wrapping a feature in a Feature does not make it supported anywhere
  it was not already.
- WireForm, Sweep and SectionChain do not accept Feature declarations.

**Scope.** Feature names resolve lexically. A Feature in a Model shadows an outer
one with the same name; a Feature inside a Struct is invisible outside it; two
definitions in one scope are an error. Calls inside a Feature resolve where the
Feature was defined. A Feature and a Profile may share a name.

**Limits.** Expansion is bounded: 64 levels of nested calls or default
dependencies, 4,096 invocations, 65,536 expanded declarations and 4 MiB of
generated construction per expansion phase. Exceeding a limit rejects the whole
program; it never yields a partly generated part.

### Naming applications

Name a call when you will refer to its result, edit it or attach anything to it:

```firmament
Modify stock {
  Feature leftBore = MountHole(center: Layout.leftMount)
  Feature rightBore = MountHole(center: Layout.rightMount)
}
```

`MountHole` is the recipe, `leftBore` is this application's identity, and
`Layout.leftMount` supplies its location. Moving the datum moves the bore
without renaming it. Reordering named applications keeps their identities,
though order still decides construction dependencies. The name gives access to
what the result kind already publishes, for example `face(leftBore.Wall)` for a
hole wall. It does not add capabilities, and it does not promise that every face
survives a topology change.

Anonymous calls get positional names (`__0`, `__1`, ...). Do not use them as
durable references; name the call first, then update any selectors that used the
generated name. Expanded fields in reports are read-only: edit the call's
arguments or the datum it uses.

## Function: a pure expression

A `Function` returns a scalar, `Point2`, `Point3` or a declared Record from its
arguments. Functions have no access to outer names except through their
parameters; a Static with the same name as a parameter does not replace it.

`Curve2` and `Curve3` bind a point-valued expression to a finite parameter
range. Profiles and other consumers turn curves into material.

- `representation: Exact` requires an exact lowering.
  `representation: Approximate` requires a positive `maxDeviation` and reports
  the geometric error bound. This budget is unrelated to `tol` and PMI.
- `Layout.Curve.At(t)` evaluates the original equation within its domain. The
  parameter is not arc length.
- `Curve2` carries an explicit plane; `Curve3` uses its definition's world frame.

See [equation-driven curves](../../firmament/equation-curves.md) for complete
examples.

## Pattern: finite repetition

A Pattern maps a finite **source** to a **recipe**:

```firmament
Model MountingPlate {
  units: mm

  Feature Drill(center: Point2, diameter: Length = 6mm) -> Hole<Shaft> {
    return Hole<Shaft> {
      on: +Z
      center: center
      diameter: diameter
      end: ThroughAll
    }
  }

  Static mountPoints: Set<Point2> {
    left => Point2(-12mm, 0mm)
    right => Point2(12mm, 0mm)
  }

  Box stock { size: [50mm, 30mm, 8mm] }
  Modify stock {
    Pattern mounts over mountPoints {
      point => Drill(center: point)
    }
  }
}
```

- Put a Pattern inside its target's `Modify`, or directly in a Model or Struct
  that has exactly one body.
- Sources can be named Sets, arrays, equal-pitch or irregular stations, or a
  Function-driven series, so not only linear and circular arrangements. See
  [Patterns](../../firmament/patterns.md) for a non-linear example.
- At most 1,024 instances.
- `=>` here binds the element name for the recipe. It is not a general lambda.
- The element name substitutes values only. It never renames fields,
  declarations, strings or similarly spelled identifiers.

**Identity.** Results from a Set are named by Pattern and key
(`mounts.left`, `mounts.right`) and keep those names when entries are inserted,
removed or reordered. Results from arrays and generated grids are positional.
`build --json` reports the generated instances under `patterns`.

Different owners use different Pattern forms. They are separate forms, not
alternative spellings of one loop, and `Item`, `Current` and an explicit element
name are not interchangeable:

| Source | Form |
| --- | --- |
| Named Set to a Feature | `Pattern name over values { value => Recipe(value) }` |
| Concept points from Linear, Stations or Series | `Pattern name over Layout.Points { point => Recipe(point) }` |
| Keyed assembly sites | `Pattern name over sites { site => <Part Member = Definition> ... </Part> }` |
| Semantic PointSet or Grid | `Pattern name { Source: layout.Points ... Item ... }` |
| Record array with a feature Template | `Pattern name over records { Recipe<Current> }` |
| Radial symmetry | `Radial Pattern name { source: seed; about: axis; count: n; angle: full }` |

In Helios, **Patterns…** edits the source layout, law and recipe, previews the
whole result and applies it as one undoable change.

## Template: specialize a product

```firmament
Template<width: Length, height: Length, thickness: Length>
Struct PlateFamily {
  Require positive => width > 0mm && height > 0mm && thickness > 0mm
  Box stock { size: [width, height, thickness] }
}

Struct standardPlate = PlateFamily<width: 80mm, height: 50mm, thickness: 8mm>
```

- A Template declares typed parameters and the kind of thing it produces:
  `Struct`, `Model`, `Concept Struct`, `Panel`, `SheetMetal`, `Profile` or
  `ProfileDelta`.
- `Require` decides whether a specialization is admitted.
- Parameters can be scalars or Records; a Record carries a whole configuration
  (see [lesson 4](../../learn/04-reuse.md)).
- Template names are lexical. A Model-local Template can shadow a file-level one;
  a sibling Model's Template is invisible; duplicates in one scope reject.
  Templates nested in a Template resolve from its definition, not from the
  caller.
- Forge Host and other tools discover file-level product Templates.
- A specialization header cannot silently drop placement or other clauses.

A separate, smaller feature-Template form is used by record-array Patterns. See
[Templates](../../firmament/templates.md) for argument types and Tables.

## Mirror and radial symmetry

Symmetry transforms construction before it is built. It never mirrors a finished
BRep or STEP file.

```firmament
Mirrored Feature rightMount from leftMount { across: centerPlane }
Feature largerMount = rightMount with { diameter: 8mm }
```

(Inside a `Modify`, with a `leftMount` Hole and a `centerPlane` declared.)

- `Mirrored Feature` and `Mirrored Profile result from source { across: plane }`
  reflect curves, restore loop winding and rebuild a right-handed frame.
  Construction planes traced from Concept planes are accepted in the Profile
  form.
- Materials, scalar values and enum values are unchanged by reflection.
  `Mirrored Material` is not an operation.
- `with` derives a feature with overrides and keeps its source and mirror
  provenance.
- A mirrored feature that would land exactly on its source is rejected as a
  redundant duplicate. A Profile lying on the mirror plane may remain as a named
  derivation.

```firmament
Radial Pattern boltCircle { source: boltSeed; about: mainAxis; count: 6; angle: full }
```

- The source is instance zero. `count` is 1 to 1,024.
- A full circle spaces instances at `i × 360°/count`, without a duplicate at the
  end. A partial `angle` includes both ends: `i × angle/(count − 1)`.
- Angles accept `deg`, `radians`, `quarter`, `half` and `full`.
- Supported for planar holes with a `Point2` centre, about their support's
  normal axis. Profiles, Boss, Pocket, whole Structs and assemblies are not
  supported.

Complete examples: [mirrored hole](../../../../fixtures/Canonical/Symmetry/mirrored-hole.firmament),
[mirror with override](../../../../fixtures/Canonical/Symmetry/mirrored-feature-with-override.firmament),
[radial bolt circle](../../../../fixtures/Canonical/Symmetry/radial-bolt-circle.firmament).

docs/public/reference/language/solids-an.markdown:
# Solids and features

A mechanical Model has **one material body**. You make it from a primitive, an
extruded Profile or a `Compose`, and then apply features to it. A second body in
the same Model is rejected at its declaration, never silently discarded. Separate
objects belong in separate parts of an [assembly](assemblies-and-motion.md).

## Primitives

| Primitive | Fields | Placement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Box` | `size: [x, y, z]` | centred in X and Y, from Z = 0 up |
| `Cylinder` | `radius`, `height` | axis on Z, from Z = 0 up |
| `Cone`, `Frustum` | `bottomRadius`, `topRadius`, `height` | axis on Z, from Z = 0 up; `topRadius: 0mm` gives a point |
| `Sphere` | `radius` | centred on the origin |
| `Torus` | `majorRadius`, `minorRadius` | centred on the origin, axis on **Y** |
| `RoundedBox` | `size`, `cornerRadius` | centred on the origin in all three axes; vertical corners rounded |
| `Ellipsoid` | `radii: [x, y, z]` (semi-axes, not diameters) | centred on the origin |
| `Polyhedron<N>` | `edgeLength` | centred on the origin |

The placements are not uniform. In particular, `Torus` lies in the XZ plane, and
`RoundedBox` is centred where `Box` sits on the XY plane. Check bounds with
`aetheris measure` when it matters, and place parts in assemblies through frames
and mates rather than relying on primitive origins.

`Polyhedron<N>` is a regular convex solid with `N` faces: 4, 6, 8, 12 or 20.
`Polyhedron<6>` has axis-aligned faces and `Polyhedron<8>` axis-aligned
vertices. Other counts reject.

`Ellipsoid` is an exact quadric. It is exported to STEP as exact rational patches
and recovered as an ellipsoid on reimport. It is symmetric; an egg shape needs a
different construction.

## Modify

`Modify name { ... }` applies features to an existing body: holes, edge finishes,
patterns, [grooves and manual ribs](../../firmament/grooves-and-ribs.md).
`Modify Base {}` with no features is a valid no-op, as long as `Base`
exists.

On a single `Extrude`, Modify takes the same features as on a `Compose` body:
holes, slots, patterns and edge finishes. The Extrude builds as
`Compose name { Base name { ... } }`. `Perforation` is for Box and hollow
Cylinder stock; on Extrude and Compose bodies it rejects at its declaration
(use a `Pattern` of holes for a grid of openings).

Angular mold `Draft` is not currently a V2 `Modify` feature. Its bounded legacy
operation does not imply support on the modern authoring path. Manual
`Rib<Rectangular>` accepts its own explicit side `draft` while constructing the
rib; that is separate from drafting existing body faces.

## Compose

`Compose name { ... }` builds a body from a Profile-based stack of operations. It
does not reopen a separately declared Box.

| Intent | Operation | Key fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting stock | `Base` | `profile`, `from`, `to` |
| Raised material | `Boss` | `on: Top` (or `name.Top`, or a `Span<Plane>`), `profile`, `height` |
| Finite recess | `Pocket` | `on`, `profile`, `depth`, optional `minimumFloorThickness` |
| Through cut | `Pocket` with `end: ThroughAll`, or `Remove` with `role: ThroughCut` | `on`, `profile`; no `depth` |
| Capsule slot | `Slot<Capsule>` | `length`, `width`, `direction`, `extent`, `role` |
| Drilled hole | `Hole<Shaft>`, `Hole<Counterbore>`, `Hole<Countersink>` | see below |

`on: Top` resolves to the current top of the material under the feature's
footprint, after the operations before it. If two equally high supports qualify,
the feature is rejected as ambiguous; name one, for example `on: pad.Top`.

A Pocket always leaves a floor. Its required floor comes from
`minimumFloorThickness`, then from an active manufacturing policy, then from a
default, and the build fails when the floor would be thinner. Do not mix `depth`
or a floor requirement with `end: ThroughAll`.

### Coaxial primitive Compose

A coaxial `Compose` can join positive-radius `Cylinder` and `Frustum` spans without sketches or Boolean union. The first span starts at the local origin along +Z; each later span names the previous span's top support, and their joining radii must match. For example:

```firmament
Model CountersunkFastener {
  units: mm
  Compose body {
    Cylinder shaft { radius: 2.85mm; height: 12.85mm }
    Frustum head { on: shaft.Top; bottomRadius: 2.85mm; topRadius: 6mm; height: 3.15mm }
  }
  Modify body {
    EdgeFinish<Chamfer> tip { on: shaft.Bottom; target: Boundary; distance: 0.5mm }
  }
}
```

This produces exact cylindrical, conical and planar supports. A chamfer on an exposed terminal Cylinder rim removes equal axial and radial distance, giving a 45° lead-in. Its distance must be smaller than both cylinder radius and height. One chamfer per exposed end is admitted. For a reusable Record/Template and assembly seat, see the [fastener library](../../../../fixtures/Regression/CodeNativeAssembly/fastener-library.firmament).

This bounded stack rejects arbitrary placements, mismatched joining radii, radial shoulders, overlapping or disjoint spans, mixed Profile/primitive operations, internal-rim finishes, Fillet, holes and part PMI on this Compose family. It also rejects typed tolerances that it cannot project. Other Compose families retain their own admitted operations.

## Holes

| Variant | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `Hole<Shaft>` | `on`, `center`, `diameter`, `end` |
| `Hole<Counterbore>` | adds `counterboreDiameter`, `counterboreDepth` |
| `Hole<Countersink>` | adds `countersinkDiameter`, `countersinkAngle` |

`end` is `ThroughAll` or `Blind <depth>`, for example `end: Blind 10mm`. A field
from another variant, such as `counterboreDepth` on a Shaft hole, is an error.

In a Compose body, all three variants are supported on the `+Z` support with
`end: ThroughAll`:

- The entry is found from the material at the hole's centre, so a taller boss
  elsewhere does not lift it. A pocket floor can be an entry only if the whole
  mouth fits on that floor.
- The entry footprint must lie entirely in material, including around pockets and
  slots. Overlapping or tangent entries and breakouts through a wall reject.
- A counterbore or countersink must leave a positive length of plain shaft below
  it. A countersink is an exact cone.
- Holes on other supports of a Compose body, and blind counterbores or
  countersinks there, are not supported.

## Edge finishes

`EdgeFinish<Chamfer>` takes `distance`; `EdgeFinish<Fillet>` takes `radius`.
`kind: Chamfer` and `kind: Fillet` are older spellings; if both a variant and
`kind` are given, they must agree. A bare `Fillet name { ... }` is not an edge
finish.

An edge finish works on the edges around one face. To round the vertical edges
of a plate or block, round the corners of its outline instead; the result is
exact and holes still apply:

```firmament
Model Plate {
  units: mm
  Profile Outline = RoundedRect2 { center: [0mm, 0mm]; size: [50mm, 40mm]; radius: 3mm }
  Extrude Plate { profile: Outline; from: 0mm; to: 8mm }
  Modify Plate {
    Hole<Shaft> Corner { on: +Z; center: Point2(19mm, 14mm); diameter: 5.5mm; end: ThroughAll }
  }
}
```

What you can select depends on the body:

| Body | Selection |
| --- | --- |
| An unmodified Box | `face: +X`, `-X`, `+Y`, `-Y`, `+Z` or `-Z` with `target: Boundary`: that face's rim |
| An extruded Profile | `target: section.Outer` or `Boundary` with `on: Top` or `on: Bottom`: the whole rim |
| A Compose body | `target: profile.Outer` with `on: Top` or `on: Bottom`, within the qualified material history below |
| An untouched Box or `Polyhedron<N>` | `target: AllEdges`, fillet only: every edge |

The details that trip people up:

- **One finish per construction.** Several finish requests on one Profile or
  Compose body reject, rather than building only the first. Uncalled Feature and
  Template definitions do not count.
- **Box rim with holes.** One Box top-rim chamfer or fillet can sit with top
  `ThroughAll` holes in the same Modify, if the hole entries stay strictly inside
  the inset top face. Blind and side holes sharing a rim finish are not supported.
  The fillet keeps sharp vertical corners; it is not whole-box rounding.
- **Compose with holes.** A top-rim chamfer can coexist with pockets and holes as
  long as its corridor does not cross a counterbore shoulder or countersink
  transition. One constant-stock Base with disjoint through round holes also
  supports either cap's fillet or chamfer, including rounded Profile corners.
  This cavity-retaining path currently requires native XY stock, a single outer
  loop and positive clearance between each entry footprint and the rim corridor.
  Blind holes, slots and additional material operations reject in that path.
- **Whole-stock rounding.** `target: AllEdges` needs one fillet, a radius smaller
  than the stock's inradius, and no other edits. It rejects on every other body,
  including Ellipsoid, RoundedBox, imported, hollow and already-edited stock, and
  it rejects an all-edge chamfer.
- **Size.** A finish must leave a non-collapsing cap. Straight polygon corners
  need not be right angles; tangent line/arc rims and arcs closed by a chord also
  work. `endClearance` is for open chains and rejects on closed loops.

The [fillet and chamfer guide](../../firmament/fillet-profiles.md) has
executable examples and explains how the planner chooses a construction.

## Combinations

That a feature exists does not mean every combination with other features is
supported. The [geometry guide](../../firmament/geometry.md) and
[supported features](../supported-features.md) list what combines. An
unsupported combination always rejects with a diagnostic; remaining geometry that
looks plausible is never evidence that everything you asked for was built.

## Regions and imported geometry

`Region` is not a general declaration. It appears in three bounded places:

- **Older mechanical source** has a lowercase
  `region sideHole on face(+X) { cut Cylinder { ... } }` inside `modify`. Use
  `Hole<Shaft>` in new source.
- **Sheet metal** names planar regions, and **FEA** selects `Region:` fields.
  These belong to their domains; see [sheet metal](../../firmament/sheet-metal.md)
  and [FEA](../../firmament/fea.md).
- **Imported STEP revisions.** `Recognize` names a region of an imported body.
  The supported workflow moves or removes one proved, complete, round through-hole
  in an imported part while keeping the rest of the BRep:
  - pin the STEP file with `sha256` (exact bytes) or `textSha256` (UTF-8, LF
    normalized);
  - select the hole by inspected candidate, for example
    `candidate: "through-hole:step-764+765"`. `aetheris imported-features inspect`
    lists candidates, and `plan --as MountHole` writes a complete revision;
  - `Replace ... with Hole<Shaft>` moves it within explicit `within` bounds (one
    box, or `[sourceBounds, destinationBounds]`), and `Remove Source.Name { within: ... }`
    deletes it;
  - `Source.Name.diameter`, `.depth`, `.center`, `.entry`, `.exit` and their
    `.X`/`.Y`/`.Z` components can be used in the edit;
  - `geometryOnly: true` is required, and excluded source annotations are
    reported.

  Limits: one move or removal per Model, along X, Y or Z, same size, between
  parallel planar faces. Slots and countersinks cannot be edited. A partial wall
  is never promoted to a complete hole. `importTolerance` controls how imported
  geometry is qualified and has nothing to do with a manufacturing `tol`. See
  [imported through-hole revisions](../../firmament/imported-feature-recognition.md).

Manual rib junctions and their admitted combinations with holes and perimeter
finishes are described in [Grooves and ribs](../../firmament/grooves-and-ribs.md#rib-junctions-and-mixed-features).

# Aetheris 2.0.0 release notes

Aetheris compiles Firmament engineering source into reviewable artifacts. The
managed CLI runs in local development and CI; the Windows bundle also includes
Cadmata and the NativeAOT Forge Host.

```powershell
dotnet tool install --global Aetheris.CLI --version 2.0.0
aetheris validate fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament --json
aetheris build fixtures/Canonical/Learn/01-plate.firmament --out artifacts/local/first-plate.step --json
```

Use the first-plate source from the [learning guide](../learn/01-first-part.md).
The compiler supports bounded exact parts, assemblies, Sheet Metal, semantic
PMI, STEP import/export, mesh export, drawings and analysis. See the
[supported features](supported-features.md) and [known issues](known-issues.md)
for the actual capability contracts.

Validation and build share domain selection. Unknown fields and unsupported
units reject at their owning binders. Native V2 `model` is a case alias for
`Model`; historical serialized inputs and `solid` grammar retain their separate
compatibility boundaries. Normal validation includes required engineering
preflight; parse-only validation explicitly reports its limited level.

The managed tool is qualified on Windows x64 and Linux x64. The self-contained
desktop bundle targets Windows x64. The public NuGet library set includes its
full dependency closure and pins Copeland's managed VTS/WGSL compiler to 0.1.0.
No Copeland checkout or private feed is needed. The core CLI has no third-party
OS-native dependencies; SQLite and 3DM remain optional adapters. Drawing Notes
use pinned PDF.js browser assets; PDF drawing output remains managed.

Forge Host Protocol v1 and the VS Code extension are independently versioned.
Cloth3D and Humanoid packages remain experimental. STEP geometry and explicitly
authored semantic PMI retain their engineering authority; assembly export does
not implicitly promote part PMI into assembly PMI.

Release assets include an inventory and SHA-256 checksums. See the
[bundle guide](../release-bundle.md) for layout and use.
